A mechanism is proposed to generate a massive Nambu-Goldstone boson that is analogous to the kaon condensation model. This model incorporates a spontaneous breaking of a $U(1) \otimes U(1)$ symmetry and a higgsing of a $SU(3) \otimes SU(3)$ global symmetry through the introduction of two types of meson fields: $\Sigma$ and $\Pi$. The resulting Lagrangian contains $\Pi^2$ terms that are invariant under the symmetries and can be used to massize the NG boson associated with the broken $U(1) \otimes U(1)$ symmetry. In the process, the $\Sigma$ and $\Pi$ meson fields develop non-zero expectation values that give rise to the mass terms and result in the $\Pi$ field becoming a massive field that belongs to the mixed branch of the meson spectrum. This model can be applied within the context of dense matter, where the Fock-Fadde'ev mechanism might be relevant, and also serves as an analogy for the proposed "diquark condensation" mechanism in dense QCD. In the process, a meson gap equation is derived and solved for the $\Pi$ field in the presence of a density-dependent $\Sigma$ field that serves as a driving term for the mass generation of the $\Pi$ field. The resulting density-dependent $\Pi$ meson mass scale is then compared to conventional models of dense matter. The impact of the $\Sigma$ field density dependence on the $\Pi$ meson mass is also examined within the context of a three-flavor scenario based on an Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model. The generated mass is found to be scale-invariant and follows a power law that is in agreement with recent empirical findings based on nuclear collective flow data. The proposed model also serves as a natural explanation for the observed mass scales based on the kaon mass itself and other relevant parameters, and as such, provides a natural explanation for the scale invariance properties of dense matter. The resulting mass scales obtained from the model are comparable to those obtained from other theoretical models based on the same NJL parameters and as such, serve as a consistent description of dense matter based on a meson gap equation. The model also allows for the investigation of the impact of the kaon condensation scenario on the $\Pi$ meson mass scale and as such, serves as a theoretical analogue for experimental searches of the $\bar{p}$/$\

Recent advances in counterfactual generation using structural causal models, specifically DISCO, have shown promise in machine learning. To test the impact of this approach on machine learning robustness and generalization, our investigation utilizes the well-established dataset OHSUMED in the context of a binary classification task. Counterfactual data was generated via DISCO, which was then used to train models with various robustness-enhancing techniques. Our findings indicate that model robustness improves significantly when training on counterfactual data, especially when interventions are extensive. Moreover, our research reveals that the beneficial effects of counterfactual data are short-lived and generalization performance plateaus at a lower counterfactual density. Additionally, we observed the impact of parameter configurations on DISCO's ability to produce high-quality counterfactual data, which is crucial for effective machine learning. To facilitate reproducibility, our research provides pre-trained models and necessary code for future machine learning robustness investigations. Our work demonstrates the value of counterfactual data in machine learning and highlights the significance of considering model robustness from a perspective that accounts for underlying causal structures. Moreover, our findings emphasize the significance of carefully selecting parameter configurations for counterfactual generation to ensure high-quality output, which is critical for machine learning models intended for real-world applications. Our research on model robustness extends beyond machine learning and has implications for various domains, including computer science, philosophy, economics, and sociology. Our code and model datasets are available at https://github.com/robustml/counterfactual_sensitivity. Our investigation follows the theoretical framework outlined in recent counterfactual research, specifically the work described in reference [][][]. Our research builds upon the DISCO framework introduced in reference [][][] and extends the analysis found in reference [][][]. Our study utilizes the OHSUMED dataset, which was previously utilized in machine learning research, specifically the findings reported in reference [][][]. Our research utilizes the BART baseline model, which was initially introduced in reference [][][] and further developed in reference [][][]. Our research incorporates robust machine learning techniques that have been individually validated in various studies, including but not limited to reference [][][][][][][][][][][][]. Our research incorporates the Cramér--von Mises criterion that was initially introduced in reference [][][]. Our investigation employs the widely accepted causal interpretation of the hospitalization counterfactual, which was initially proposed in reference [][]. Our research extends the findings related to machine learning robustness described in reference [][][] and extends the generalization research described in reference [][][]

Researchers synthesized epitaxial materials on graphene substrates and observed the presence of distinct coexisting domains, which were influenced by the growth temperature and method of synthesis, as analyzed using X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy. Below 750°C, a material with a spinel structure grew in two different orientations, which were in competition with each other, while temperatures above 800°C resulted in a single cubic material structure. This temperature-dependent transformation was attributed to an intermediate oxide layer and varied with the synthesis method, offering a level of flexibility in material design and synthesis. Furthermore, computational simulations supported the findings and revealed the crucial role of thermal diffusion and the reordering of atoms during material growth, which was in line with experimental results. This study demonstrated a precise and scalable method of fabricating multifunctional materials and epitaxial domain control at the atomic level, which has significant implications for the development of advanced energy harvesting technologies and high-performance electronics. This breakthrough synthesis of a temperature, chemistry, and site-controlled material was found to occur on a low-cost, versatile graphene platform, which enables the fabrication of controlled domain materials in bulk quantities, presenting a significant technological advancement, and is particularly influential in the field of spin electronics and energy harvesting applications. A major challenge in supervised learning algorithms for multi-label classification lies in their slow pace due to the extensive annotation required for labels. A key aspect to overcome this limitation is generating high-quality multi-label data at a lower cost. In this paper, a novel technique called single-to-multi-label (S2M) sampling is developed to create affordable multi-label data in large quantities. The proposed method initializes a sample with one randomly chosen relevant label, and then uses a learned model to determine the probability of each remaining label being relevant. These probabilities are then utilized to guide random selections, ensuring they adhere to the original data distribution. The effectiveness of the S2M sampling method is demonstrated through two significant applications: (1) producing pseudo-multi-label data for model enhancement, and (2) creating real multi-label data at a reduced cost. Experimental results across both use cases show a significant reduction in annotation costs required to achieve the same classification performance as traditional methods. The proposed S2M sampling method is implemented as a learning-based model and made available for public use on GitHub. Code for model training, as well as example usage, is also publicly available. On large-scale multi-label classification datasets, the proposed technique demonstrates the ability to achieve a 10-fold increase in generated data with only a 2-fold increase in training costs. The developed model can be utilized with a wide range of learning-based models, including both graph-based and kernel-based methods. The paper also presents theoretical support for the proposed S2M sampling method by examining label co-occurrence patterns through the lens of a widely accepted model, the independent Bernoulli model. Experimental results show the proposed technique's versatility, with successful pseudo-multi-label data generation using a random model and real multi-label data creation using a strong learning model. The developed model's ability to adapt to novel distributions is further validated through both shift tests and generative adversarial network-based attacks. The paper's contributions are threefold: a novel single-to-multi-label (S2M) sampling technique is introduced, demonstrating the feasibility of efficient pseudo-multi-label and real multi-label data generation, with the potential to produce super-large-scale multi-label data at minimal costs. The paper also presents theoretical insights into the proposed technique through the analysis of a widely accepted model, and assesses the proposed technique's robustness through distribution shift tests. The code for the paper can be found at https://github.com/zwang84/S2M. The model for the paper can be found at https://github.com/zwang84/S2M

Within this category, we discover that the weakly natural adjunctions form a full subcategory of the natural adjunctions. Furthermore, we establish that the category of natural adjunctions exhibits the same properties as the category of functors that preserve limits. These conjugate functors are revealed to be strong natural transformations between the original functors. The paper also delves into the relationship between conjugate functors and the topological categories that they induce. A key discovery made in the paper reveals that the category of conjugate functors displays the same level of 'topological-ness' as the original categories from which the functors were derived. To explain the significant gamma-rays beyond 1GeV observed in some beams dumps, a new model is proposed that attributes variable electron heating rates to specific turbulent fluid motions. Although the standard, self-consistent model can accurately match the majority of gamma-ray data, those that exceed GeV necessitate additional physics and offer opportunities to assess the variability of electron heating. Utilizing detectors with high-energy sensitivity, such as the MAGIC telescope, allows for a more precise understanding of the gamma-ray spectrum in beam dumps and serves as a sensitive indicator of the variability of electron interactions with a turbulent environment. A Monte Carlo simulation-based simulation framework already established is expanded to incorporate the new model and a range of magnetic field variations, which is essential for validating the MAD model's predictions against real-time beam data. By applying this framework to recent LHC fills where variable electron beams interact with a pre-existing, turbulent magnetic field, the most probable electron heating rates were determined to range from 10^-3 to 10^-2, and the associated distributions are presented with an exploration of possible explanations. The research showcases a novel and promising approach to investigating the variability of electron interactions with a turbulent environment and serves as a pioneering effort in a newly emerging field of beam physics research. Medical applications involving wearable devices often face challenges due to user privacy concerns, requiring sensitive health data to be kept confidential.  A prominent issue in addressing this problem is that wearable activity recognition typically relies on centralized data storage, compromising user privacy.  To address this challenge, a novel decentralized framework called FedHealth has been developed to facilitate the recognition of wearable activities on devices without accessing sensitive data.  Through a mechanism of incremental learning on individual devices, FedHealth enables a secure and private determination of wearable activities without centralized data access.  The results of experiments conducted indicate that FedHealth succeeds in enhancing the accuracy of activity recognition in a wearable system compared to conventional approaches, achieving a significant improvement of 11.6% in activity recognition accuracy on average.  Furthermore, FedHealth exhibits a notable improvement of 25.2% in activity recognition accuracy when data is decentralized, based on experimental findings.  The framework also shows scalability, with a notable reduction of 93.1% in communication costs for model updates, facilitating seamless deployment across various devices.  The code of FedHealth has been made publicly available to support future research and development in wearable activity recognition systems. Portfolio risk management is a critical task for investors seeking to minimize both portfolio risk and returns. The complexity of this problem makes it difficult to tackle on its own, hence the investigation of optimization approaches that consider multiple objectives and utility functions to effectively manage portfolios. This study explores seven distinct optimization approaches, classifying them into utility and multi-objective optimizations, examines the underlying theories and utility functions used, and reviews various numerical and empirical studies to ensure the validity and practicality of these methods in real-world applications. A particular highlight is the examination of utility-based and multi-objective optimisations in relation to portfolio performance, considering both classical and modern perspectives including machine learning. The findings of this study are expected to serve as a foundation for future research aiming to enhance portfolio performance through the application of advanced optimization techniques, and to provide investors with accessible and effective optimization methods in increasingly complex and dynamic financial markets. The review process encountered a few challenges in modeling portfolio performance risk due to the scarcity of such studies in machine learning, deep learning, and finance. This review is intended for both academic and practical purposes, offering valuable insights for investors, financial industry professionals, and young researchers entering the field. The task-to-set paradox, where an optimal set must be found within a set of possible sets that vary in size, has implications for algorithmic problems including panel creation and interview scheduling. Researchers have proposed various techniques to circumvent the task-to-set paradox by utilizing a larger set of possible sets, however, these methods are often inefficient for large-scale problems. This study introduces a novel two-stage approach to solve the panel creation problem, a specific instance of the task-to-set paradox, in a manner that considers multiple possible sets of any size. The algorithmic solution, with a time complexity of O(|E| + |P|^2) and a second-stage linear program of type B, provides optimal results for small problem sizes and scalable performance for large problems respectively. Experimental findings demonstrate superior performance of the proposed algorithm in comparison to existing methods, with notable improvements in solution quality for large-scale problems. Furthermore, additional research on the panel creation problem involves an examination of the relationship between problem size and key performance indicators, uncovering both linear and step functions. This study also explores various algorithmic strategies for finding optimal sets of varying sizes, offering valuable insights into possible circumventions of the task-to-set paradox. Experimentation with real-world recruitment data showcases the algorithm's effectiveness and highlights potential challenges with application in real-world scenarios. This study's contribution is further highlighted by the novel two-stage algorithm being applicable to a broader task-to-set paradox class than existing research, with the added benefit of being efficient for large-scale problems. This study's findings are complemented by a case study of a recruitment agency conducted in collaboration with the organization, providing valuable real-world insights into panel creation and task assignment. This research's outcomes are relevant to various applications involving set creation from possible sets of different sizes, offering a versatile algorithmic solution. This study's empirical component is distinguished from existing research by the use of linear program of type B in the second stage, in addition to the consideration of multiple possible sets of any size in the first stage. This study's limitations are acknowledged with opportunities for future research including the analysis of a single-stage algorithm that considers multiple possible sets of different sizes and an examination of type B linear program's performance in comparison to type L linear program. This study's findings also highlight the need for further research on algorithmic approaches that consider multiple possible sets of different sizes, with potential applications in various real-world scenarios. Our investigation focuses on the asymmetric production of leptoquarks, a phenomenon that could occur at the LHC, given that certain missing energy signatures are present, potentially linked to new physics. To explore this possibility, we develop a general framework that incorporates various leptoquark representations and asymmetric production mechanisms, both for first and second-generation particles. A key requirement for this investigation is a well-defined 2-TeV $ee$ collider with a missing energy detector, allowing for the study of both same-sign and opposite-sign lepton production. As a result, we are able to derive asymmetric $s$-channel production equations that relate leptoquark masses to collider energy, further analyzing how charge asymmetry affects the behavior of these particles at different energy levels. Moreover, our analysis highlights how a distribution of charge asymmetry can serve as a key indicator for identifying leptoquarks at such a collider. By utilizing these findings, we are able to determine the minimum mass at which leptoquarks can be discovered at a 2-TeV $ee$ collider, under both ideal and realistic missing energy conditions, offering valuable insights into the capabilities of such a detector in uncovering this particular type of new physics. Our study also highlights the significance of considering charge asymmetry when investigating leptoquark behavior at an $ee$ collider. In the course of this research, we recognized the need for a new equation that describes the behavior of scalar leptoquarks in the context of the standard model, leading to a calculation of the decay width of these particles, a crucial step in modeling their asymmetric production correctly. Our investigation into the behavior of leptoquarks at a 2-TeV $ee$ collider also led us to propose an adjustment that enhances the reach of such a detector for these particles, further highlighting the importance of charge asymmetry in this context. Our research provides a comprehensive foundation for the study of leptoquark behavior at future $ee$ and $e\gamma$ colliders. Our code for the asymmetric production equations presented in this research is available upon request. Our results for the minimum mass required to discover leptoquarks at a 2-TeV $ee$ collider, along with the distributions we analyzed, are also available in the supplementary material for this paper. Epidemiological modeling is increasingly dependent on differential equation modeling, which is often solved to obtain the incidence and other key variables of interest. Although these models are typically fit to available epidemiological data, there is a lack of consideration for an essential aspect: biological feasibility. In reality, there are limits to how rapidly a population's infection and death rates can change, and there are maximum and minimum bounds to the sizes of infected and removed populations. Furthermore, there is often a minimum time required for a significant change in the infection and removal rates. In this work, we introduce a new method for estimating these rate bounds and time scales from partial and potentially incomplete data, which is achieved through the use of a nonlinear regularization technique applied to the solutions of the differential equations. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through simulations and real-world applications to SIR and SEIR data sets. The resulting models are then used for forecasting future trends and comparing them with traditional methods, which shows that the proposed method provides more realistic and accurate predictions. The implementation of the proposed method has been made available in the RODENT package on CRAN, which can be accessed at the following address: https://cran.r-project.org/package=RODENT. Our research demonstrates how a non-rigid pendulum can mimic the intricate behavior of a specific atomic configuration under magnetic fields, ultimately leading to atom-molecule conversion. By developing an efficient "hidden" model, we've uncovered the underlying dynamics and precise instability thresholds, and our results indicate that this description is effectively approximate, with a precision determined by the rigidity of the pendulums. By paraying our findings, we've an upgraded model with a higher precision, which we've applied to a specific atomic state and numerous drive protocols, both continuous and discrete. This has allowed us to map the boundaries of instabilities and identify the conditions under which molecule formation occurs, in both its single- and multi-photon forms. Our study reveals the intricate interplay between the dynamics of a quantum system and its environment, leading to the formation of novel, Fock-state molecules even in the presence of white noise, and reveals how specific magnetic field patterns can delay the onset of instabilities and molecule formation, in addition to the well-known effects of varying the strength of the magnetic field. Our effective model also highlights the significance of pendulum curvature in the dynamics of atom-molecule conversion, and how certain configurations can result in the creation of two coexisting molecules from one atomic condensate. Finally, we've investigated the role of pendulum curvature in the formation of novel, bound atom-molecule pairs, and the requirements necessary to achieve long-lived atom-molecule entanglement. Our research provides a new perspective on the dynamics of atom-molecule conversions and reveals the vital role that pendulum curvature plays in the formation of molecules from a quantum system driven by a magnetic field. Our findings are applicable to a wide range of atomic species, including the commonly studied $^{87}$Rb and $^{85}$Rb atoms. Our non-rigid pendulum model has the capability to extend our research to more complex atomic configurations, and our methods are versatile enough to be adapted for the study of other driven quantum systems that exhibit nonlinear behavior. Our discovery of the effective non-rigid pendulum model has facilitated our understanding of the intricate dynamics of a specific atomic configuration under magnetic fields, and has allowed us to gain insight into the atom-molecule conversion process and the onset of instabilities and molecule formation in a quantum system. Our research demonstrates how an efficient non-rigid pendulum can mimic the behavior of a particular atomic configuration in magnetic fields, ultimately leading to atom-molecule conversion, and provides a new perspective on the dynamics of this process. As DNA data storage evolves, managing external readings becomes an escalating concern. Reducing the number of storage partitions is a viable solution to address this issue, but it also makes data retrieval less accurate. This paper addresses an important problem affecting precision in data recovery and presents two primer pair design strategies to minimize the number of partitions: examining read patterns to avoid overlapping extensions, and selecting non-overlapping primer pairs from the start. Our results show that using a strategy for non-overlapping designs reduces the number of partitions by half in some cases, resulting in a successful 100% data retrieval rate from previously inaccessible 12-base partitions when using 20-base partitions. Furthermore, our findings indicate that applying this strategy can shorten data reading time by up to 30%. Our approach has been incorporated into an existing system, leading to an improved performance where a higher data density is now possible with the same reading time, or a reading time is achievable with the same data density. Our proposed approach has been made open-source for the community to further modify it as needed. System developers and researchers are welcome to collaborate and improve this design further with different synthesis strategies. Our initial findings provide a foundation for future improvements in primer pair design, aiming to increase data accuracy in DNA data storage by reducing the number of storage partitions. Our proposed approach has been tested using standard DNA sequences found in NCBI and synthetic sequences with varying GC contents. Our research discovered important relationships between these elements and our design strategy, offering valuable insights for the community. Our analysis also reveals the maximum scalable partition size as a function of read patterns and sequence lengths, providing a necessary guideline for future DNA data storage systems development. Our proposed approach has been made available on the following link: https://github.com/aliyazdani/dna-primer-design. Precise knowledge of riverbed geometry is crucial for managing water resources and preventing floods, but accurately measuring bathymetry throughout an entire riverbed is impractical due to its vast extent. Typically, measurements are taken at various points along the river, and a statistical method is used to fill in the missing information. The development of hydrodynamic models enables bridging the gap between local measurements and a complete, detailed bathymetric map. In this research, a new statistical approach called PCGA is introduced to enhance model predictions when applied to rivers with extensive sandbars. By accounting for spatial variability and incorporating flow velocity data, PCGA enhances model predictions for riverbed depth. When compared to the conventional approach, PCGA yields better results in model predictions, especially for model-based predictions. Furthermore, PCGA outperforms conventional methods in both low and high flow conditions the rivers in this study experienced. The PCGA method has additional benefits, including the ability to produce a variance map that indicates areas with high bathymetric variability and prioritizes areas for additional measurements, and flow velocity data can be replaced with other relevant measurements to increase model accuracy. The PCGA method has a straightforward code structure that allows easy customization and incorporation into existing water resource management frameworks. A significant improvement achieved with PCGA is the reduction of computational time required for modeling rivers with extensive sandbars, demonstrating its practical value for real-world applications. The PCGA method has been made available through an open-source platform for water resource management, known as pygama, which also houses the code for other related projects, and can be accessed from a public repository on GitHub. The future development of PCGA aims to enhance model predictions further by incorporating additional relevant data, such as aerial photographs and satellite imagery, and assessing the scalability of PCGA to other types of rivers and geographies. Recently, a significant amount of research has focused on enhancing image quality through the integration of multiple images with varying exposure levels. Although algorithms like CEDD, LEICA, and MRF-based approaches have yielded impressive results, their reliance on time-consuming computational processes and limited generalizability across new scenes poses a problem for real-world applications. To address this challenge, researchers have explored deep learning solutions, yet these methods typically require a vast amount of high dynamic range HDR image data, which is hard to obtain and often results in models learning unnecessary features rather than a realistic HDR representation. This study addresses this challenge by developing a novel external exposure prior network that incorporates a self-imposed exposure regularization mechanism to produce more realistic and diverse HDR images with less training data. The proposed method successfully generates high-quality HDR images using a limited dataset of mere hundreds of images. Moreover, it is shown to be robust in new scenes and can be used with a single HDR image for scene-aware image editing. The results provided outperform current state-of-the-art deep learning methods according to the metric MS-SSIM. The proposed method also compares favorably to several state-of-the-art algorithms, including CEDD, LEICA, and MRF-based approaches, based on the MS-SSIM and VGG-M objective assessment measures. The code for this research is available on GitHub at the URL https://github.com/zhongyury/EPPNet.

Causal deep learning methods aim to incorporate causality principles into neural networks, yet the breadth of these methods has outpaced the depth of research assessing their limitations and future directions. To gain insight into this field's shortcomings and potential areas of study, we evaluated research on causal deep learning through the lens of established methodologies and theoretical frameworks, identifying noticeable gaps in current research. Specifically, we found a lack of studies examining the causal implications of overfitting, batch normalization, and universal representation learning within neural networks. Consequently, we propose several theoretical models and empirical studies to fill these research gaps. For example, we developed a stochastic context-switching model to demonstrate the causal origins of overfitting during context-switching and presented a theoretical context-switching probability to highlight the causal effects of hyperparameter choices. Furthermore, we investigated several natural language processing tasks and found that they are affected by context-switching, likely contributing to the low success rate of previous research. To address this challenge, we introduced a novel context-switching learning framework that incorporates a context-switching layer to enhance robustness against context-switching and validated our approach on multiple tasks, resulting in improved performance. To facilitate further research, we publicly released our context-switching dataset and learning framework at https://yichengxu.github.io/projects/cs_learning/. In topological terms, the Madsen-Weiss theorem states that the moduli space of genus $g$ mapped surfaces under homotopy classes that are compatible with a given orientation-preserving homeomorphism has a specific structure. Initially proven by Peter Ogus using an integral formula, his demonstration was reworked by Claudio Munoz to show that the Madsen-Weiss theorem falls under the category of the b-principle. As a result, various generalizations were possible, leading to the development of a method for connecting the Madsen-Weiss theorem to the Chern-Weil construction. This connection enables the derivation of the Madsen-Weiss theorem from the Gauss-Manin connection and subsequent applications in calculating via spectral sequences the Betti rational cohomologies of moduli spaces of surface mappings. Additionally, this approach facilitates a geometric interpretation of the Chern-Simons invariants used in the calculation. By linking these results to the topological Torelli theorem and its generalizations, a connection to the Gauss-Manin connection's role in calculating cohomologies of moduli spaces of curves and surface mappings becomes apparent. A particular focus is also given to how these findings relate to the development of a geometric strategy for defining the Chern-Simons invariants from surface mappings, allowing for a direct interpretation of the resulting invariants as integrals of differential forms along curves within moduli spaces of surface mappings. A key aspect explored in this research is how the relationship between the Gauss-Manin connection and these Chern-Simons invariants enables the derivation of key properties, including their degree 1 property, invariance under reparameterization, and relationship to the Kodaira-Spencer obstruction theory. A notable outcome of this research is the accessibility it provides to an advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate-level audience, with the content based on a combination of existing knowledge and key contributions from the field of topological surface mapping research. A key aspect highlighted in this work is the role of the Chern-Weil construction in connecting the surface mapping moduli space's geometry to its topology, with key implications for understanding and applying the surface mapping's moduli space geometry. A key aspect explored in this research is the relationship between the surface mapping's moduli space geometry, defined by the Weil-Petersson metric, its properties, and the relationship to the Kodaira-Spencer obstruction theory, with key outcomes including a degree 1 property and invariance under reparameterization. We develop a new analysis of the Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) preconditioner, focusing on a non-nested version that is suitable for unstructured finite element grids. The performance of the BDDC algorithm depends on various factors, including the number of degrees of freedom in the subdomains, the number of degrees of freedom in the interface, the choice of local solvers, and the coherence parameter. We investigate how these factors influence the condition number of the preconditioned system and present sharp estimates in a model problem. Leveraging these findings, we derive more general bounds on the condition number that account for non-uniform subdomain sizes and non-nested grids. We also explore different coarse space dimensions and local solver choices. To validate our analysis, we apply the BDDC algorithm to a realistic problem involving structured and unstructured elements, and compare our theoretical predictions to numerical results. Our results demonstrate a strong correlation between predicted and actual condition numbers. To improve the preconditioner, we modify the BDDC algorithm by adding extra degrees of freedom to the coarse space, which significantly reduces the number of iterations required to solve the linear system. We analyze this variant and demonstrate its improved performance. Our numerical experiments showcase the practical benefits of this variant, especially when solving large-scale problems. To obtain these results, we first developed a way to accurately count the number of degrees of freedom in the subdomains and the interface from the generated finite element grid, which we also present as a related contribution. This approach can be used to create more efficient finite element grids by minimizing the number of interface degrees of freedom. We believe these developments will be valuable for a broader range of linear solvers and finite element grid methods. Our BDDC algorithm implementation is an instance of the Algebraic Domain Decomposition (Al-DDC) class, and we explored its relationship with other algebraic methods, including Ruisch's variant and the algebraic FETI method. Our findings on the impact of the coherence parameter are particularly significant, as it enabled us to determine an optimal value based on the condition number analysis, which in turn allowed us to achieve a 30% reduction in the number of iterations when solving a real-world problem. We also found that our implementation of the BDDC algorithm is highly efficient when compared to other distributed solvers, with a 20-30% faster solve time for similar problem sizes. Understanding how particles diffuse in complex systems like live tissues, polymers, and plasma is crucial for comprehending various fundamental and applied phenomena. A widespread approximation in such studies posits that Brownian motion is unhindered by correlations and variations among the particles' mobilities, and instead follows a straightforward Gaussian pattern. While this assumption holds approximately in some cases, deviations from it could significantly impact our overall understanding. A recent study found that when applied to a specific model of interacting particles, Gaussian diffusion assumptions were violated in a way that resulted in an anisotropic, non-equilibrium state. The initial research identified the source of this behavior as the unusual distribution of the particles' velocities and the resulting counterflow that prevents them from diffusing apart. The aim of this new study was to see if the same dynamics that led to those results could sustain the anisotropic state over a wider time scale, and to determine if the state could become equilibrium state and what kind of equilibrium state it would be. The new research used numerical simulations to repeatedly run the model with the same parameters, and it found that the anisotropic state often remained for a relatively long time compared to the time it took the particles to cross over from correlated to uncorrelated velocities, but ultimately converged to a state of equilibrium that was counterintuitively rotationally symmetric. The reason for this symmetry was the uniform distribution of the velocities' directions, which the researchers verified through additional simulations where the initial direction of the velocities' distribution was different. The new study also looked into how the rotationally symmetric equilibrium state changed over time, and found that the increase in the particles' mobilities' variations accelerated the decrease in counterflow, but the rate at which the velocities lost their directionality remained constant, indicating that the directionality would always take the same time to lose in the conditions used. The aim of the new study was also to see if the same dynamics that led to the initial state could be repeated, and it found that the conditions under which the same dynamics could be repeated were very strict, mainly because the initial state had a specific distribution of the velocities' components that was difficult to achieve, but also because the time it took to achieve the same state again was long compared to the time it took the particles to cross over from correlated to uncorrelated velocities. We investigate the interplay between self-phase and cross-phase modulation in a loop resonator that contains identically counterpropagating light modes with non-zero phase differences. A theoretical model is developed to analyze these nonlinear effects within a loop that comprises two identical, lossless cavities connected in series. By applying a dimensionless variational approach, we are able to compare the strengths of the self- and cross-phase modulation. It is found that the self-phase modulation coefficient is always greater than the cross-phase modulation coefficient, with the latter being exactly twice the former when the initial phase differences between the counterpropagating modes are zero. This advantage can be realized by employing a loop that contains Kerr media loops in counterpropagating configurations. This phenomenon holds true regardless of the level of nonlinearity within the resonator. A theoretical model is then applied to a specific loop configuration that exhibits nonlinear behavior, and this is verified through numerical solutions of the coupled Schrödinger equations. A loop resonator that exhibits nonlinear behavior can serve as a fundamental component for implementing nonlinear effects over extended periods of time, and this has been demonstrated through both theoretical and experimental means. This includes the creation of coherent solitary waves, as well as their dynamic formation and dissolution, by employing both continuous-wave lighting and dark pulses of light. This specific study highlights the distinct advantages of cross-phase over self-phase modulation in a loop resonator that contains counterpropagating modes with zero phase difference, and this can be harnessed to increase the nonlinear threshold of the resonator. This, in turn, allows for the successful implementation of nonlinear effects over extended periods of time through a loop resonator. This can be achieved by incorporating additional loop configurations that contain Kerr media in co-propagating modes with a fixed phase difference, in addition to loops in counterpropagating configurations. This enables a loop resonator to serve as a nonlinear amplifier that has a high threshold, and this can be utilized to amplify nonlinear phenomena that occur over a range of power levels. This is made possible by adjusting the phase difference between the counterpropagating modes to match the specific nonlinear application at hand. This can be done by varying the temperature of the loop through thermo-optic means, or by adjusting the mode matching through beam manipulation, without any degradation of nonlinear properties over time. This has been demonstrated through both theoretical and experimental means, and this includes the successful amplification of nonlinear phenomena that occur over a wide range of power levels, from very low levels to very high levels. This study introduces a novel super-resolution GAN model that incorporates multiscale information to enhance resolution in turbulent flow simulations. A key aspect investigated was how the model adapts to different Reynolds numbers, specifically Re=15000 and Re=18000, in turbulent channel flow. To account for varying viscosity, the model was adjusted by changing the number of multiscale layers. Results showed that the model effectively maintained predictive accuracy of turbulent velocity distributions when model parameters were fixed, even across different Reynolds numbers. Furthermore, the model successfully enhanced low-resolution snapshots of velocity fields at different resolution levels, both with and without noise. Notably, when trained on sub-vortex scale data, the model could predict both sub-vortex and super-vortex scale velocity distributions with high accuracy. Lastly, model predictions for streamwise velocity distributions showed excellent agreement with experimental data from Kaneda (2003), both at the bulk flow scale and the sub-vortex scale. A comparison with a standard GAN model revealed inferior performance, both in predicting bulk flow velocity distributions and in maintaining model stability. A proposed assessment of GAN training convergence helped clarify its limitations. To facilitate reproducibility, the source code and model data have been made publicly available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/JasonIshihara/mssr-GAN. A key finding highlighted the model's ability to capture intricate turbulent velocity distributions, despite being trained on relatively coarse data, making it a promising tool for enhancing resolution in high-dimensional turbulent simulations. Reevaluating a reinforcement learning algorithm involves comparing it to alternative policies under various scenarios of educational content, which can be challenging due to the high dimensionality of state-action pairs. To tackle this issue, a controlled modification is proposed that utilizes a value function to assess the quality of actions in a given set, thereby enabling a more efficient comparison of different policies. This innovation is demonstrated to yield meaningful and comparable results when evaluating multiple policies across various educational settings. The proposed approach provides a framework for comparing policies that is both adaptable and rigorous, and its advantages are showcased through the evaluation of state-of-the-art learning algorithms in controlled policy environments. In these controlled settings, subtle differences in algorithm performance are highlighted, and the relationships between their strengths and weaknesses are illustrated. The value of the proposed framework is further underscored by enabling the extraction of policy generalization as a trainable problem, and this is illustrated through a supervised learning experiment that reveals both accurate and principled gains from employing curriculum-based data sets. The resulting value function at this level can be utilized to guide future learning in dynamic environments, which is also explored in a experiment with a changing educational plan. The code and results for all experiments are available at https://github.com/DeepFactorization/rrl_eval. The approach introduced in this research can be applied to controlled policy environments found at various locations including DeepMind Lab, Seismic Talk, and Atari 260 games. Process mines that depict processes' structural characteristics can change significantly in response to various factors over time.  A key challenge arises in uncovering the time-dependent evolution of process structures when observational data is available across multiple time periods.  A major limitation of current process mining techniques is their inability to handle situations with multiple instances of the same process type being observed in different time frames.  In processes comprising complex tasks and varied structures, time-independent techniques often struggle to deliver accurate results.  To address these limitations, a novel method is proposed for discovering time-dependent processes from semi-structured data, specifically event streams.  This approach yields a time-dependent, structured model, enabling exploration of the process's temporal evolution through a range of analytical tools.  A real-world example is demonstrated, illustrating how this method can be applied to uncover the time-dependent development of a critical business process within a large telecommunications company.  A subsequent evaluation through simulation validated the method's performance in relation to changing process rates and durations.  Furthermore, a theoretical analysis is provided of the model's accuracy in relation to its parameter, $\Delta t$, which represents the minimum time period required for distinguishing process changes.  This is accompanied by empirical data on the optimal $\Delta t$ values for different process scenarios.  The proposed approach is an important advancement in process mining, offering a flexible framework that can be employed in diverse settings, from those described above to other process evolution scenarios.  The resulting time-dependent DCR graphs can be made available for public use through the Bannish website, along with the necessary tools for further analysis.  Future applications of these models are envisioned in areas such as process improvement and prediction, in addition to evaluation of process mining techniques against real-process data.  Future research directions are also explored, including the development of time-dependent techniques for discovering task hierarchies and analyzing process performance through weighted models.  A time-dependent extension of the Heuristics Miner is also proposed, along with guidelines for selecting suitable processes for this approach and the description of generated models as well as evaluation results.  The necessity of considering process time evolution in process mining is highlighted, along with the limitations of current time-independent techniques in capturing complex processes.  A theoretical analysis of the proposed approach is also provided, offering insights into model accuracy in relation to its parameter, $\Delta t$.  The advantages of semi-structured data over structured data in process mining are also discussed, along with the challenges and potential applications of using such data in process mining scenarios. We uncovered a significant discrepancy in NUV-r colors for low-redshift galaxies observed by GALEX and a previous study by Salim et al. (2007), specifically for galaxies with a mass of approximately 10^9.5 solar masses or more. A distinction in colors emerged at this mass threshold, with larger colors observed for galaxies above this threshold. This phenomenon remains unexplained and suggests that stellar populations in these galaxies may be different from those in lower mass galaxies. Alternatively, environmental factors such as mergers or central black holes may be influencing these results. Furthermore, a shift in colors was observed for galaxies with a high mass, emerging about 1-2 Gyr after the present time and persisting into the current era, and could indicate that these galaxies adhere to a universal evolution path. If this evolution is universal, it would imply that massive galaxies always exhibit larger NUV-r colors and specific luminosities in the near ultraviolet spectrum. If this is the case, it would support the theory that these galaxies evolve in a manner that is consistent with their mass, possibly through mergers that occur over the course of the age of the universe. This analysis held the luminosity in the near ultraviolet spectrum constant and found that the minimum mass necessary to observe the discrepancy in NUV-r colors also depends on the rate of star formation, being 10^9.5 solar masses for galaxies with a low specific star formation rate. This implies that galaxies with higher specific star formation rates, such as blue compact dwarf galaxies, do not exhibit the same colors and may have different evolutionary paths. This analysis also compared different mass functions of galaxies and found that those with the largest NUV-r colors are more likely to follow the Kroupa mass function rather than the Salpeter mass function. If the definition of red sequence galaxies is based on color, then this discrepancy occurs over a period of about 1 Gyr and results in about 20% of galaxies becoming part of the red sequence each Gyr. If the definition of red sequence galaxies is based on specific star formation rate, then this discrepancy occurs more rapidly, with about 40% of galaxies becoming inactive each Gyr. This activity decline can be observed over the entire age of the universe and may indicate a universal evolution for all massive galaxies that started the journey. If this is the case, it would be challenging to identify true satellite galaxies without knowing their prior history of mass and star formation. Recently, machine learning models have demonstrated a high level of accuracy in natural language processing tasks, with a particular emphasis on translation and multilingual text classification. However, these models tend to exhibit poor performance when applied to languages they haven't been trained on, with some showing limited ability to effectively utilize their trained capacity across multiple languages. This paper introduces a novel neural transfer technique, which enables the use of pre-trained models in unfamiliar languages by leveraging the inherent relationships within the world's language spectrum. A custom multi-head attention mechanism is developed to facilitate seamless cross-lingual knowledge sharing, with the potential to expand classification tasks beyond initially trained language datasets. Notably, this approach allows models to successfully navigate unfamiliar languages without the need for additional training, with results showing significant performance improvements in text classification across 8 diverse languages. When applied to zero-shot language scenarios, the method demonstrates remarkable classing accuracy rates of 25.1% on mean F1-score. This achievement surpasses the current state-of-the-art zero-shot model performance by a considerable 6.1%. As healthcare systems face significant challenges in managing limited resources during the COVID-19 pandemic, it's essential to allocate them effectively, especially for patients in intensive care units.  To this end, we propose a novel approach that predicts the duration of patients' ICU stay and identifies key factors influencing their progression in the ICU.  Unlike previous studies, our approach accounts for the impact of admission characteristics on patient outcomes and resource requirements.  By analyzing specific features related to ICU admission, our approach determines their relative significance in predicting ICU discharge and identifies those most crucial for discharge, which in turn can be used to prioritize resource allocation.  We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by developing an interpretable machine learning model that accurately forecasts ICU stay duration and assigns weighted importance to admission characteristics, thereby facilitating informed decision-making about resource allocation for COVID-19 patients in the ICU.  Our findings highlight the significance of admission characteristics in predicting patient outcomes and highlight potential applications in optimizing healthcare delivery. The classical result by Kan and Thom stating that the universal bundle functor over a simplicial set is natural with respect to simplicial mappings can be reinterpreted through the lens of category theory as the result of applying a specific monad to the simplicial set's homotopy group functor. This paper provides an alternative proof of this reinterpreted statement. Additionally, it establishes a connection between the simplicial group's universal bundle functor and the standard simplicial group monad. By leveraging this connection, the paper shows that the natural transformation resulting from the application of the simplicial group monad to the simplicial set's homotopy group functor is equivalent to the image of the standard simplicial group monad's application to the trivial simplicial group functor, mapped via the natural equivalence that holds between the standard simplicial group monad and the category's free functor. A final conclusion drawn from this analysis is the observation that the universal bundle functor corresponds to the image of the free simplicial group functor applied to the simplicial set in question. This latter result can be viewed as a natural extension of the fundamental group's property being equal to the image of the free group functor applied to the simplicial set. In the context of reduced simplicial sets, an analogous statement holds true. This paper also explores and establishes the universality that results from applying the standard simplicial group monad to the homotopy group functor for both regular and reduced simplicial sets. A related discussion is included to clarify that this standard monad's specification, when applied to the homotopy group functor, yields the universal bundle functor as its image. A subsequent examination of this monad's properties enables the derivation of a more general framework that can be used to define and study the universal bundle functor for any given functor mapping homotopy groups to groups. This study is found to be invariant under the choice of model for the homotopy group functor. A notable model exclusion is the fundamental group of the circle, which is instead considered to form a distinct monad. A separate examination of this monad reveals that it satisfies a group-like property known as being a monad of group type. Systematic use is made of the category theory principles, specifically the formalism associated with the algebraic theory of monads, Kleisli categories, and the standard simplicial group monad, to derive the desired universal bundle functor's properties. To mitigate the balanced negative sampling problem's significant computational cost, multiple proposal sampling strategies have been proposed, all aiming to improve models' optimization efficiency in Visual Relationship Detection. The most effective approach thus far involves ranking proposed relationships by their scores and prioritizing positive and highly scored negative samples for suppression. Building upon this progress, we present a new strategy called Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS). BNPS divides negative samples into three distinct groups: (excluded) highly scored, (suppressed) moderately scored, and (rejected) low-scored, and systematically explores the optimal splitting points for maximum model performance. Utilizing a designed search procedure, BNPS finds the ideal split that balances model performance against the cost of sampling, achieving notable improvements over existing methods. We demonstrate BNPS's advantages on a large VRD dataset, MontgomeryECD, obtaining a 3.4% improvement in AP over the current state-of-the-art. Our findings provide valuable insights into the optimal balancing of negative samples for model performance and computational efficiency, offering a crucial step towards addressing multiple proposal sampling's limitations. Our code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/yangzw17/BNPS.

Our research explores how galaxies formed and evolved, with a focus on the impact of accretion streams and gravitational interactions on their physical development. Using high-resolution, high-stability hydrodynamic simulations, we investigated the effects of different gas stream densities and distances from the galaxy's center on the distribution and movement of the galaxy's mass components. These components included the primary galaxy, the accretion stream, and a small satellite galaxy that underwent disruption. As the galaxy absorbed the incoming gas streams and the broken-down satellite, its physical development responded in various ways, with different streams producing distinct results. A closer look at the disk and the bulge revealed how the distribution of mass shifted in response to the incoming streams, leading to changes in the galaxy's overall structure. Specifically, we observed an increase in the bulge-to-total mass ratio and a transformation from an optically faint, irregularly shaped galaxy to a brighter, more ordered system. This transformation occurred because the galaxy's central bulge grew through both the merger of the satellite and the inhomogeneous distribution of the absorbed gas streams, with the outer regions absorbing the gas from the streams and the satellite, and then expelling it in a combination of fast-moving winds and slower, more diffuse streams that contributed to the galaxy's disk. As a result, the galaxy's physical development was marked by a central bulge growth and the formation of a disk from the consumed and expelled gas components. This process was similar to that observed in major galaxy mergers, but with key differences, including a slower bulge growth and greater stability, making it another possible pathway for galaxies to develop their structure and evolve during their formation. This process is particularly relevant for galaxies classified as "quenched" or those with a low specific star formation rate, as it provides an alternative explanation for their development, with key features that can be observed, such as a central bulge, a minimal disk, and little to no satellite galaxies remaining. This research opens the possibility of studying these galaxies formed through interactions with gas streams and satellite galaxies that break down, through the analysis of their chemical composition, using abundance ratios derived from spectroscopy. This would allow a better understanding of how galaxies formed and evolved, with a focus on those that were once actively forming stars, as it offers a more complete explanation for their current state of inactivity. This process is also worthy of further simulation with different variables, such as galaxy masses and different gas stream densities, as well as the inclusion of supermassive black holes. A highly intense X6 solar flare along with widespread coronal mass ejections occurred on November 7th, 2004, causing significant disturbances in the interplanetary medium and enabling the study of high-energy particle accelerators in the solar atmosphere. As a result, abundant cosmic rays were observed at Earth, reaching levels that exceeded background by over a hundred times, and allowing for an in-depth examination of their effects on the upper atmosphere and terrestrial electricity. Utilizing a ground-based network of electric field sensors, variations in the electric field were recorded at multiple locations on November 7th, 2004, revealing temporary reductions in the daytime built-up negative surface electric field at low latitudes, and similar decreases in the negative surface electric field at higher latitudes, though these occurred at different times. These findings indicate that high-energy solar particles can cause a temporary collapse of the built-up negative surface electric field during intense solar events. Additionally, atmospheric ionization led to a global redistribution of atmospheric charge, resulting in a sudden increase in the global atmospheric potential, which was recorded as a positive spike in the surface electric field at multiple locations on November 7th, 2004. This atmospheric potential spike was found to be directly proportional to the cosmic ray intensity and the local surface air density, offering a means of remotely sensing the global atmospheric potential from solar cosmic ray variations. It is also proposed that during intense solar events, the global atmospheric potential can become sufficiently large to drive electrical discharges into the atmosphere, and their recorded signals could be mistaken for those originating from the solar wind, and that variations in the global atmospheric potential could influence terrestrial climate by driving atmospheric electrical processes that in turn affect local temperature, as seen in the post-storm warming phenomenon. It is further suggested that high-energy solar particles can cause a permanent alteration in the upper atmosphere and terrestrial electricity, as indicated by the observed decrease in atmospheric potential following the 2004 event, and that there might be existing evidence of this effect on the atmosphere and Earth's magnetic field from historical solar flare events. It is also proposed that terrestrial climate variability could be influenced by the interaction between the interplanetary medium, the upper atmosphere, and terrestrial electricity, as described by a combined magnetohydrodynamic atmospheric electric circuit, and that this circuit could drive atmospheric electrical processes that affect local temperature, and may have contributed to post-industrial era global cooling and current warming trends. It is also observed that there are notable correlations between solar flare energy releases, cosmic ray variations, and both atmospheric electrical processes and terrestrial climate,

KIC 9267654 is a solar-type star that was found to possess an unusual internal rotation profile when first studied in 2013. Its distinct slow and fast rotation zones are separated by a radical 1.5 solar radius wide boundary, which could result from various phenomena such as external gravitational influences, star-eating interactions, or localized energy dissipation. To further investigate this intriguing phenomenon and consider possible explanations, we conducted a thorough analysis of this star's behavior over time through a study of nearly seven years' worth of data from the Kepler space telescope. By examining how the star's frequency varies with time, we discovered minimal alterations in its internal rotation pattern despite notable variations in its light intensity. Specifically, we observed that the boundary that separates the fast and slow rotation regions remained remarkably stable over the nearly seven-year period, with a variation of less than 0.05 radians. If the star is indeed in a binary system, our calculations suggest that its companion must have a significant impact to maintain this rotation boundary, and we also found that the star is likely to be slightly sub-massive, with a mass that is merely 0.98 solar masses, and it exhibits subtle oscillations that deviate from the standard characteristics observed in solar-type stars. If confirmed, KIC 9267654 would represent a crucial discovery in the study of close binary star interactions and localized energy dissipation within stars. Furthermore, it could also provide a unique explanation for the formation of eccentric giant planets, as it presents a possible 'pre-eclipsing' stage before a binary star system reaches the Algol stage. Given its distinctive characteristics and relatively stable rotation boundary, we advise targeting KIC 9267654 for further study with instruments that can probe variable star interactions and precise mass measurements, such as TESS and Gaia. If observed with sufficient precision, its eccentric orbital period could also be detectable, which would allow us to calculate its minimum orbital period and determine if it is, in fact, a 'pre-eclipsing' star. If this is the case, it would make KIC 9267654 an ideal target for studying close binary star interactions before they reach the Algol stage, and also provide a unique opportunity to study the interplay between binary interactions and the migration of eccentric giant planets. If not, its precise mass and orbital period could still offer valuable insights into close binary star interactions that result in localized energy dissipation and variable star rotations. The explosive spread of fake news on social media during emergency situations can be mitigated if emergency management professionals can quickly identify false information.  To efficiently achieve this, a intelligent agent is proposed that utilizes enhanced deep learning capabilities to effectively detect fake news.  This detection capability draws upon the information both text-based descriptions and sentiment data associated with a piece of news, both originating from the social media platform and being influenced by how the public reacts to it.  A novel deep neural network, MetaFEND, is developed to address these complexities and an optimized framework, MDSD, is created to handle both meta-learning and sentiment integration effectively.  Through extensive testing, MetaFEND demonstrates the highest accuracy in detecting fake news to date.  In contrast to conventional approaches, this agent also requires a reduced amount of training, enabling real-world deployment among dynamic and ever-changing social media information.  Ultimately, this intelligent agent is designed to be utilized in emergency situations by leveraging the theory of planned behavior to make data-driven decisions on what information to believe and what actions to take.  As a result, it can be an invaluable resource for managing emergencies and public health crises.  The code for MetaFEND is available at https://github.com/zhongyuyu/MetaFEND.  Future developments of this project are being worked on at https://github.com/aisdc. This paper investigates a one-dimensional periodic transport equation with nonlocal flux and no dissipation. Contrary to similar equations with local flux, we find that the proposed equation yields unusual results for specific types of initial data, including smooth odd functions. Initially, these data generate solutions with distinct behavior on opposite sides of the period and solutions that eventually become infinitely steep in finite time. Furthermore, we observe that any non-zero odd perturbation about these solutions will grow without bound, leading to a unique unstable mode. To study this unique instability, we engage in a stability analysis via Fourier methods, leveraging the symmetry to significantly narrow the spectrum of functions requiring examination. As a result, we determine that only a specific odd frequency becomes unstable and that its growth can be precisely quantified. Leveraging these findings, we derive a modified equation for the combined dynamics of this unstable frequency and the remaining stable modes, which surprisingly resembles the standard Kuramoto-Sakoda equation seen in other transport equations. Ultimately, we demonstrate that this new perspective offers a more direct proof of the results initially obtained via a stability analysis. Additionally, we observe that this new perspective allows the inclusion of local terms, whereas the original equation description excluded them, thereby preventing a convergence issue. Moreover, we note that the local terms introduced do not alter the unique characteristics of the instability but instead accelerate the solution's approach to steepness. To conclude, we also examine the limitations of our stability analysis to related problems with similar characteristics. Hone's recent work allows us to extend our results to certain periodic domains that are not one-dimensional. In these domains, we find that only specific modes are unstable and that their combined dynamics is analogous to the one-dimensional case. Consequently, we are able to draw conclusions about the unique instability of the corresponding reference solutions. In particular, we demonstrate that the solution's unique instability is not a local phenomenon and that it eventually leads to a state of uniform steepness, which we term a shock state, thus confirming the initial conjecture that the transport equation will converge to this state from any initial data that is not odd. In contrast to the one-dimensional case, we are unable to determine the time scale for the solution's approach to the shock state due to the wider range of unstable frequencies available in higher dimensions. In addition, we investigate the transport equation with a source term and find that this source can significantly accelerate the solution's approach to the shock state, whereas local terms generally reduce the time required but do not alter the overall state of the solution. A quaternary Golay complementary array pair can be conceptualized as a pair of complete quaternary arrays sharing the same index set, with the property that their combinations yield two Golay sequences when measured over a specific set of points. For a Golay sequence to exist within the real numbers, the dimension of the array must be an even number. A quaternary Golay complementary array pair can exist in a complex space if the array dimension is any odd number, denoted as 2n-1. A quaternary GCA pair in a complex space with arrays of dimension 2n-1 is equivalent to a binary GCA pair in a complex space with arrays of dimension n-1. A quaternary GCA pair in a complex space with arrays of dimension 2n is equivalent to two binary GCA pairs in a complex space, one with arrays of dimension n and the other with arrays of dimension n-1. A fundamental challenge in machine learning for complex systems involves developing techniques that enable efficient recovery of a system's underlying structure from observations, particularly when these observations take the form of time series data. A probabilistic graphical model, specifically a Bayesian network, is an effective tool for capturing the intricate relationships within a system, however, accurately recovering its underlying structure from temporal data is a difficult problem. In a setting where only limited prior knowledge about the network's structure is available, we developed an efficient algorithm that leverages this information and incorporates time series observations to infer the network's structure. This algorithm, in turn, draws upon a novel optimization-based approach that enables the incorporation of soft constraints, thereby accommodating noisy and incomplete data. We demonstrated the efficacy of our method through comprehensive experiments conducted on various real-world datasets, including those from the fields of biology and finance. These experiments showcased our algorithm's capacity to yield accurate results even when data is highly noisy or substantially incomplete. In addition, a thorough theoretical analysis was conducted to establish an upper bound on the number of samples required to ensure the consistency of our algorithm's estimated network. This consistency was further empirically validated through experiments conducted on synthetic data. In summary, the algorithm developed in this research provides an effective solution for recovering a Bayesian network's structure from time series observations, offering a valuable contribution to the field of machine learning for complex systems. In a related but distinct problem, we also explored the challenge of recovering a discrete, hidden healthcare diagnosis from time series physiological data, presenting a novel approach that incorporates prior healthcare knowledge in the form of a Bayesian network. This approach led to the development of a new metric that quantifies the impact of prior knowledge on classification results, thereby facilitating an empirical comparison of different knowledge incorporation methods. In the experimental evaluation conducted, our novel approach was found to yield superior results when compared to alternative methods. In addition, all experiment code has been made publicly available on GitHub at the specified URL. In another aspect, we also investigated the difficulties encountered when applying standard deep learning techniques to a critical healthcare diagnosis task that involves classifying discrete healthcare codes from time series physiological data, experiencing a substantial drop in performance when using models pre-trained on large datasets containing unrelated time series data. In an effort to address this challenge, we developed a novel deep learning framework that incorporates prior healthcare knowledge in the form of an atlas, thereby enabling the distinction between diagnostically relevant and irrelevant temporal information, and facilitating an accurate classification of healthcare codes. This note presents a few new results from stable homotopy theory that can be understood by utilizing graded polynomial rings and their properties. Some proofs suggested here are speculative and are based on Geisser's advice. We begin by explaining how a particular collection of partitions can be used to define a descending sequence of graded polynomial rings. This leads to the derivation of a descending sequence of local rings at a specified prime number. We then examine the relationship between these local rings and certain groups of integers. A particular result concerning one specific prime number, namely 3, is also presented. This involves the use of a specific sequence of graded polynomial rings that results from a particular type of $Ext$ calculation, which yields information about the structure of certain groups of integers. A final section explores how these developments are connected to the properties of a specific family of spaces known as Milnor's exotic $\mathbb Z_2$-spaces. This discussion includes a description of how these spaces are related to graded polynomial rings and the role of number theory in their homotopy type. A key conclusion drawn from these findings is that all of Milnor's exotic $\mathbb Z_2$-spaces have the same homotopy type and this homotopy type can be determined using the values of Dirichlet characters at specific complex roots of unity. Moreover, we demonstrate that these spaces have a specific property - they contain a factor that is highly connected and maps onto a sphere with a certain size. This result was initially proven by Milnor for the prime number 3, while for other prime numbers, the relevant data is derived from number theory and the associated groups of integers. A final section examines the relationship between these graded polynomial rings and the cohomology of the exotic $\mathbb Z_2$-spaces, which in turn reveals information about the associated groups of integers and their relationship with number theory. This discussion is accompanied by some speculative comments on potential connections to Motivic cohomology. A novel convolutional neural network-based model has been developed to automate the precise identification and categorization of specific lung nodules in computed tomography scans by tackling both object segmentation and classification as a unified problem. The proposed framework, incorporating a nested U-Net architecture, efficiently extracts both the precise boundaries of individual nodules and a comprehensive overview of the surrounding environment through dual branches, thereby facilitating efficient nodule segmentation. Furthermore, a feature extraction module has been integrated into the network to capture both global and local characteristics, thus enhancing both classification and segmentation performance. Experimental evaluations based on LIDC-IDRI, a widely used dataset containing 759 scans with ground truth for 299 single nodule scans, demonstrated improved performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods, achieving a dice similarity coefficient of 0.857, a mean absolute error of 0.043, and an accuracy of 0.945 in classification. The proposed framework has been successfully applied to large publicly available medical datasets, showcasing its versatility in this domain. The code for this research has been made publicly accessible on GitHub at the address https://github.com/Chenyue89/ResNet-NestedUNet. The current limitation of the model requires a relatively high computational resource, with an estimated cost of 3.68s and 1.58GB per forward pass on a Tesla V100 16GB. The future scope of this research includes incorporating temporal information from sequential scans to enhance both segmentation and classification performance. The developed code and datasets used in this research are publicly available, offering a foundation for future medical image analysis research, specifically in lung nodule analysis, which can be accessed via https://github.com/Chenyue89/LungNoduleAnalysis.
