Deep neural networks have achieved high accuracy in various classification tasks due to their superior representation learning capabilities. However, their complexity and requirement for manual feature extraction make them less practical for tasks that require feature extraction before classification, especially in scenarios with limited data. This paper introduces a novel, unsupervised/supervised feature extraction framework, based on a adaptive denoising autoencoder, that efficiently learns compact and accurate representations from data. The proposed framework successfully addresses both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks by incorporating a dimensionality reduction technique and a regularizer to prevent overcomplete representations. The results of this paper were previously published in the 2020 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, but the supplementary material was newly generated for this submission. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate the proposed framework's capability to yield both unsupervised and supervised features that excel in classification tasks, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods. The code and pre-trained models for this study have been made available online for the benefit of the research community. The proposed framework's superiority is also visually represented in a feature extraction accuracy vs. dimensionality plot. The results show the proposed framework's ability to maintain high feature extraction accuracy at significantly reduced representation sizes compared to existing methods. A proposed algorithm aims to enhance decorative line rendering, specifically improving the appearance of line joins, strokes that connect at various angles, and strokes that split and rejoin, by taking into account their spatial relationships. The technique prioritizes rendering the most visually significant line segments first, utilizing a method to determine an optimal rendering order that adhers to artistic guidelines such as minimizing overlap, maintaining symmetry in joins, and avoiding the combination of certain line configurations known to yield poor results. The algorithm modulates the opacity of lines after rendering to account for external edges and prevent them from being obscured by other strokes, further ensuring that the most visually significant segments remain visible. The results shown in high-resolution, low-speed train journey animations highlight the algorithm's capacity to maintain line integrity and prevent fragmentation over time. The proposed approach has been integrated into Adobe Illustrator according to the developers' feedback. The technique's effectiveness across various fonts, with examples from ancient and modern styles, is demonstrated. The algorithm's utility extends beyond line art, as it can be applied to the rendering of branching trees in natural scenes. The proposed algorithm has been made available online for others to use. The evaluation method proposed in this research can be applied to assessing other rendering algorithms for line art. To analyze the complex dynamics of Rayleigh-B\'enard convection through multiple interfaces, researchers have developed various multi-interface models. A basic two-fluid model has particularly gained attention recently and has been shown to effectively explain various strange bifurcation phenomena observed in convection patterns near critical conditions. However, a critique of this model is that it predicts a linear heat flux increase with the temperature difference, which contradicts the observed scaling behaviour in single-interface RBC. Nonetheless, the proposed two-fluid model can also produce the observed scaling when a key assumption about the interface's symmetry is relaxed. Specifically, when there is a slight asymmetry, the model predicts the heat flux will scale with the square root of the temperature difference, similar to the results found in experiments with multiple interfaces. In this study, we further investigate the effects of interface asymmetry, specifically by adding a step to the potential fitting interface height in the model, which allows us to better align the model's results with those observed in experiments with interface mass transport, and also allows us to evaluate the model's sensitivity to this aspect of its initial conditions. Moreover, we successfully apply the two-fluid model to a scenario with three interfaces and obtain the predicted heat flux scaling, which can be further compared to future experiments with multiple interfaces. Additionally, the model predicts that melting the upper interface will result in a loss of the spinodal decomposition, which is observable in 3D but not in 2D. Moreover, by varying the density ratio between the two fluids, we are able to map the model's results onto those obtained in single-interface RBC with different aspect ratios, which can range from very small to very large. In such cases, the model predicts the heat flux scaling in a way that is consistent with the results found in the respective interface conditions. We investigate the conditions under which a cavity coupled to an individual atom generates multipartite entanglement among multiple atoms in different cavities. Due to an unavoidable loss of coherence to an uncorrelated atom, a cavity can only be used once to create non-classical states. We analyze various techniques for reviving the cavity to its initial state and utilize a single cavity to create multipartite entanglement among three atoms in different cavities. The requirements for successful generation are examined in different scenarios of cavity-coupling and damping, as well as in the presence of imperfectly initialized atoms. The role of quantum operations like displacement, Gaussian unitary transformation, and dephasing is also explored in both single- and multi-cavity setups. The study reveals that careful selection of quantum protocols is necessary to balance the generation of non-classical correlations and the destruction of coherence in the atoms. The results demonstrate the limitations of a single cavity in creating multipartite entanglement and highlight the significance of developing efficient methods to overcome this constraint, potentially through employing multi-cavity setups. The investigation provides specific conditions for achieving multipartite entanglement and offers a framework for evaluating the performance of various quantum protocols in this context. The study's findings are further applied to investigate the performance of both deterministic and Nondeterministic quantum protocols in generating multipartite entanglement from a single cavity. The investigation emphasizes the significance of developing efficient methods to overcome the cavity's limited lifespan and offers a systematic approach for evaluating the performance of these protocols based on the entanglement generation rate per cavity use. The study reveals that both deterministic and Nondeterministic protocols have the potential to generate multipartite entanglement from a single cavity, although this is always at the expense of destroying the cavity's ability to create non-classical states on subsequent uses. The investigation demonstrates the importance of balancing the creation of non-classical correlations with the destruction of coherence in the atoms and highlights the need for developing efficient methods to revive the cavity, potentially through the development of reliable sources of cavity-coupling and the creation of efficient quantum protocols that can effectively balance this constraint. The study's findings are valid for both single- and multi-cavity setups and provide a framework for evaluating the performance of these setups based on the entanglement generation rate per cavity use. We introduce a novel method to analyze the behavior of entanglement in complex optical systems using optical tomograms. This approach allows us to investigate how entanglement evolves over time, even in scenarios where a complete description of the system's dynamics is unavailable. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by applying it to a non-reciprocal interferometer and a ring resonator, both exhibiting non-accumulative entanglement and approximately maintained entanglement, respectively. Furthermore, we observe that the rate of entanglement loss in the non-accumulative case is directly related to the amount of lost coherence between the system's states. This connection provides a means of assessing the impact of decoherence on entanglement in these systems. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between our defined entanglement measure and other metrics, including the trace norm and the Hilbert-Schmidt norm, as well as their respective rates of change. This analysis enables a comprehensive understanding of the entanglement's evolution and its connection to the system's overall dynamics. Knowles et al. previously examined the relationship between the trace norm and the Hilbert-Schmidt norm in relation to the system's Hilbert space, but our findings represent a distinct and independent contribution. We also demonstrate how our approach can be applied to investigate the behavior of entanglement in a type of laser cavity, known as a Levinson cavity, where the mirrors have a non-uniform phase shift applied between them, leading to the creation and destruction of entanglement at specific frequencies, as well as the minimum amount of loss required for entanglement generation and the maximum amount of phase shift that maintains entanglement, even in the presence of a population inversion decay. This analysis provides valuable insights into the requirements for creating and sustaining entanglement in these systems. Our method also enables the investigation of the effects of changing the system's parameters on its entanglement behavior. For example, we examine how changing the cavity length, the frequency of the laser, and the phase shift applied to the mirrors influence the amount of entanglement present and how these effects evolve over time. This knowledge can be used to optimize the design of these systems to maximize entanglement generation and maintenance. Our approach provides a means of investigating the behavior of higher-dimensional entanglement in optical systems, even in the presence of lossy channels, as well as the effects of these channels on the system's dynamics and its resulting entanglement. We demonstrate our method's applicability to a wide variety of systems and scenarios

The surge in video consumption through immersive devices has highlighted the problem of poorly predicting viewer attention within videos. Various approaches have been explored to improve viewport prediction, but video subtitles remain underutilized in these efforts. Typically considered supplementary information, subtitles actually contain crucial details that can influence how users engage with content. This study investigates the value of subtitles in this context and presents a novel attention prediction model that leverages them. By incorporating subtitles into a spatial attention pattern, the proposed model significantly boosts viewport prediction accuracy by an average of 16.1% for live videos and 12.5% for pre-recorded videos. Furthermore, it demonstrates the value of subtitles in a scenario where limited information must be prioritized from videos. This is particularly relevant in applications like video summarization and streaming platform recommendations. Experimental data was collected from real users to validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. This includes multiple videos across both categories to ensure the generalizability of the results. This study's novel model and associated evaluation procedures provide a foundation for future work aimed at fully exploring the relationship between subtitles and viewer attention. This includes possible extensions to improve model performance, such as utilizing additional audio information and refining the proposed approach to handle situations where subtitles are not always present. This study is an initial step towards unlocking the untapped potential of video subtitles in this important and rapidly evolving field. This research was part of a larger thesis that also covers related video evaluation studies and a proposed framework for future work that includes possible extensions and related research in the field. A novel type of highly efficient approximation called PEPOs has been developed, enabling a drastic reduction in bond dimension while accurately mimicking both thermal states and time-evolved behaviors within quantum many-body systems. The key advantage of PEPOs lies in their ability to maintain a dimension that scales polynomially in relation to the number of system particles, both for approximating thermal states and time-evolved behaviors, and furthermore exhibits an upper bound that is finite for closed quantum systems. The development of PEPOs builds upon a previously introduced approximation method known as PEPS, and the achievement of a finite upper bound for the bond dimension is made possible by the application of a recently established theorem that enables the approximation of time-evolved behaviors using a specific PEPS-based method. The efficiency of PEPOs is demonstrated through application to a quantum Ising model and a related Dicrentralize XY model. The created approximation framework offers considerable advantages over other established methods, all while adhering to the fundamental limitations imposed by the Haahcylinder renormalization process. The resulting PEPO approximations exhibit the ability to accurately replicate both thermal states and time-evolved behaviors within various quantum many-body systems, achieving a significant reduction in required bond dimension in comparison to other widely used approximation techniques. The corresponding code for the examples and approximation framework is available at: \url{https://github.com/QSysNat/PEPO}. The original research presented in this study was featured in the paper ``Approximating Quantum Many-Body Systems with Efficient Pure-Pure-Xi Approximations'' which was published in Phys. Rev. X, see \url{https://journals.aps.org/prx/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevX.12.031064}. The development of PEPOs also builds upon the results established in the paper ``Approximating Quantum Many-Body Systems with Efficient Pure-Pure-Xi Approximations'' which was featured in the proceedings of QIP 2022, see \url{https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.00516}. The created PEPO approximations can be used within various applications such as quantum simulations, thermal state preparation, and time-evolution simulation, and the corresponding code is designed to be highly extensible and flexible. We introduce a novel method that integrates Taylor series expansion and canonical surface analysis to better understand the decoupling of partial differential equations. By applying this combined framework to the weak Hessian equation, we obtain a decoupling time estimate of $C\cdot R^2$ for initial data with a maximum Hessian norm of $R$. This result is significant because it improves upon previous estimates achieved through different methods and also provides a first glimpse of the decoupling phenomenon in the context of the weak Hessian equation. In particular, we find that our estimate is proportional to the square of the initial condition's size, a feature that sets our result apart from the linear proportionality often seen in other PDEs. In addition, our analysis offers a way to update previous scaling estimates for the solution to the weak Hessian equation, settling an open problem posed by Velazquez. Moreover, our research on the weak Hessian equation serves as a starting point for studying the Nirenberg-Taylor equation, for which we derive a similar decoupling time estimate of $C\cdot R^2$. Notably, this estimate comes with a added benefit of providing a means to update the initial data's size estimate from a given solution to the Nirenberg-Taylor equation, a feature that is not readily available via other methods. This new approach also enables us to establish local existence and uniqueness results for the Nirenberg-Taylor equation in the presence of smooth initial conditions, expanding upon the domain of existence established by another researcher. In particular, we find that our approach allows us to extend the domain of existence from the $\mathcal{C}^0$ norm of $2$ to the $\mathcal{C}^0$ norm of $0$, denoted as $\mathcal{C}^0(0)$, a key result that our analysis terms as a "smoothness gain". The traditional analysis of asymptotic series leads to an uncertainty of the same order as the perturbative expansion, with implications for recent precision measurements, such as those made in $B$-decays. A novel approach, using the mathematical concept of renormalons, allows this uncertainty to be reduced to a lower order, with an estimate of the uncertainty becoming $O(\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^2)$ rather than $O(N_{\rm f})$. This improvement is demonstrated through the example of the strange quark distribution in the nucleon, with an estimated value of $[x s(x)]_{\rm ave} \simeq 0.46 \times (0.78+0.87 \cdot \frac{\alpha_s(\mu^2)}{\pi})$ for a specific $\mu$ value. Knowledge distillation is a significant technique for reducing a large model's complexity by substituting it with a smaller, efficient model. The standard knowledge distillation approach relies on the model's soft labels, which are derived from its output. Alternatively, we introduce a novel perspective on knowledge distillation, which we've termed "decision-based black-box knowledge distillation" or DB3 for short. In DB3, the focus is solely on how the model makes decisions, without considering the underlying distribution of its output. As a result, DB3 can efficiently distill a model that operates on a black box, yielding a smaller model that excels in classification tasks. To achieve this, DB3 leverages the model's predictive outcomes for a specific task that are obtained via the model's output, and applies them to train a smaller model via standard knowledge distillation. We test DB3 under different scenarios, including using a model as a black box to train another model, and find it delivers a more efficient model while maintaining performance comparable to traditional knowledge distillation methods. Specifically, when applying a strong model as a black box, we find that DB3 allows us to train weaker models that were previously impossible to train via knowledge distillation. System codes and knowledge distillation codes are available at: https://github.com/zhoupengui/DB3_KD.

We introduce Co-Imitation Learning, a novel framework that enables agents to acquire imitating policies in multiple tasks with only general reward signals. Unlike conventional methods requiring demonstrations for guidance, our approach enables agents to exchange information about their policy updates, facilitating the transfer, especially when expert demonstrations are hard to obtain. Theoretical proof shows that an agent using Co-Imitation Learning can achieve optimal policy update rates for multiple tasks, outperforming traditional state-of-the-art methods, such as decentralized policy optimization, even without task identification. When task identification is possible, our approach can still be advantageous, offering a significant improvement over this method as well. We further provide a general update rate threshold, which, when exceeded, guarantees policy update rates comparable to those obtained using demonstrations. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments with high-dimensional control and symbolic domains, achieving notable improvements over the existing methods. Our findings demonstrate the efficacy and versatility of Co-Imitation Learning. Code for our approach is available at: https://github.com/Chenyuhong/NIPS19_CIL.

We develop a new approach to analyze the error probability of a sequential decoder that uses a polarized cutoff rate as a bias value. This method simplifies the problem by breaking it down into two independent components: a "close-to-optimal" subset and a "far-from-optimal" subset. We establish an upper bound on the error probability of the sequential decoder and demonstrate that it can be expressed as the product of two independent probabilities. This allows us to derive a simplified expression for the maximum cutoff rate that ensures a sequential decoder's error probability remains below a given threshold. We also investigate the relationship between this maximum cutoff rate and the polarized cutoff rate that maximizes the decoder's reliability, finding it to be the average of the polarized cutoff rate and its lower bound, both of which can be estimated from the channel's covariance matrix. We apply this analysis to a memoryless Gaussian channel and a parallel Gaussian channel with independent input signals, obtaining explicit expressions for the maximum cutoff rate that guarantees a low error probability. We then compare these results to the polarized cutoff rate that achieves the highest decoding success rate and find that it is more conservative by the square root of the number of channel uses. We also consider a binary symmetric channel with two levels of reliability and find that the maximum polarized cutoff rate is $\frac{h_2(1-\sqrt{p_0 p_1})}{2}$, where $h_2$ is the binary entropy function. We conclude by discussing the connection between polarized cutoff rates and the success probability of a maximum-likelihood sequential decoder on a binary symmetric channel. We identify its lowest value, determine its corresponding polarized cutoff rate, and examine its relationship to the channel's covariance matrix. We then explore the behavior of this lowest polarized cutoff rate as the success probability approaches zero or one. We find that for a memoryless Gaussian channel, this lowest polarized cutoff rate increases with the number of channel uses and is asymptotically $\frac{1}{2}$ for large enough numbers of channel uses. We establish this result by analyzing the set of near-optimal sequences and demonstrating that they become increasingly independent of each other as the number of channel uses grows, with a mutual information that is asymptotically $\frac{1}{2}$ times the number of channel uses. We compare this to the maximum polarized cutoff rate that can be achieved with a large but fixed number of channel uses and find that it is more conservative by a factor of the square root of the number of channel uses. This study delves into the examination of snapshot isolation variants observed in MongoDB's WiiredTier, Replicaset, and ShardedCluster implementations. To facilitate this analysis, we developed WIREDTIGER-IS, a comprehensive test suite focusing on database concurrency controls and specifically designed to assess MongoDB's isolation properties. Our findings reveal several previously undetected concurrency control behaviors in MongoDB. In response to these discoveries, we propose enhancements to its current configuration settings. Furthermore, we created a theoretical framework for classifying snapshot isolation variants based on their treatment of phantom reads and disk updates. This framework has been successfully applied to provide concrete recommendations for improving MongoDB's concurrency control. In one proposed improvement, we suggest a specific variant, which we term "early snapshot isolation", to address observed behavior and offer a potential fix to the problem of read skew caused by disk updates. To validate our results and test the improved variant, we developed a synthetic database concurrency benchmark known as ConcurDB. This benchmark emulates read-write workload stress tests and measures the performance differences between different MongoDB deployments and variants of snapshot isolation. Our research demonstrates tangible performance gains from adopting the early snapshot isolation variant, along with other recommended configuration changes, in various MongoDB deployment scenarios. In particular, we found that using the FsyncLock duration set to 20 milliseconds yields the best balance between performance and concurrency concurrency controls in MongoDB. In addition to its direct applicability to MongoDB, our research on the treatment of phantom reads and disk updates can be applied to other database deployments employing snapshot isolation. Our test suite, benchmark tool, and research findings are available at https://github.com/Tinlin96/mongodb-isolation. This public repository also includes our study's supplementary materials. To ensure the scalability of our research, we intend to continually update our test suite, benchmark tool, and findings to reflect any future developments in MongoDB. In this spirit, we invite the MongoDB community to engage with our research, provide feedback on our findings, and consider our proposed improvements for future database deployments. In this regard, we have already collaborated with MongoDB's development team and contributed our research findings to their issue tracker at https://jira.mongodb.org/company/main. A key property of chromatic symmetric functions under the standard basis is their positivity in a specific sense. Within this framework, we redefine the $e$-basis such that the coefficients align with the structure of the Schr\"oder tree. This enables us to establish a positive structure associated with the $e$-basis and demonstrate that certain polynomials, which initially have non-negative coefficients when expressed in the standard basis, take a positive form in the $e$-basis. This achievement is an extension of a similar result initially obtained by Garsia and Stanton through a different approach. As an additional contribution, we reexamine the relationship between the standard basis and the $e$-basis from a bijective perspective, uncovering a connection that underlies the structure of the Schr\"oder tree. This connection facilitates a computation of the coefficients in the $e$-basis in a manner that reflects the tree's path properties. We investigated an Ising model on a frustrated triangular lattice to uncover the effects of temperature-dependent coupling constants on its magnetic properties. By analyzing the interactions' symmetry, we discovered that the hysteresis loop's shape transforms from a square to a rice grain-like form through a first-order phase transition, driven by the critical temperature at which the loop's square shape forms. Furthermore, we found that the loop's transformation is governed by two distinct scaling laws, depending on the direction from which the loop's shape transition is approached, and these scaling laws relate the loop's shape to the energy required to change the magnetic field. Our findings were obtained through extensive Monte Carlo simulations of the model and were confirmed by analytical arguments related to the scaling behaviors of our simulations. By comparing our results with previous works, we rule out any unique contributions from the triangular lattice geometry and frustrations, attributing the loop's shape transformation to the external field's drive across a first-order phase transition. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the interactions between spins in a triangular lattice's 2D version and offers predictions for the scaling behaviors observed in experiments on 3D triangular lattices. Moreover, we propose that our model can be applied to a wide range of discrete symmetries often found in Condensed Matter Physics. Our results originally appeared in the paper's details.

Recent studies near the Sun discovered a higher-than-expected frequency of highly
energetic particles, requiring significant electric potential to overcome solar
electromagnetic influence. To compare this to the experience of detecting similar
energy levels at 1 AU, we examined 12 intense events from 2019 to 2022 using
multiple satellite data. Analyzing 1472 solar proton events, we found that the
energy distributions remain largely similar at different points near the Sun, with
some exceptions observed during intense storms like on March 20-29, 2017, yet even
these distributions are still capable of being explained by existing models when
accounting for varying detection efficiencies. Conversely, the number of extremely
high-energy events (above 100 MeV) is substantially lower closer to the Sun, with
a decline rate of approximately 0.6 log units per AU, and variations in the
energy spectra of the solar sources are distinct and correlated with each other. 
Based on our findings, we propose that extremely energetic events originate from
localized sources on the Sun, while the majority of protons are released from 
global, homogeneous areas with varying energy outputs, and these results also 
suggest that the electric potential necessary to accelerate the particles varies 
considerably, with a minimum required potentially exceeding 20 V for some events. 
Furthermore, our research indicates that the energy distributions require 
non-thermal acceleration mechanisms, while also implying that charged particles 
could be subject to electromagnetic influence from a vast, connected solar 
atmosphere. 
Finally, our analysis yields a crucial insight, that the energy of the most 
energetic 4% of particles remains relatively stable, with an average of approximately 
33 GeV, and a distribution that adheres to a power law of -1.24 ± 0.13. This 
distribution can be compared to others observed at greater distances, such as those 
detected on interplanetary spacecraft like Voyager 1 and the Advanced Composition 
Explorers (ACE and ASE), and even on the surface of Mars, yet with a notable 
difference in the lower energy limits. 
With our results, we aim to contribute to a broader understanding of the solar 
sources of charged particles and the energy distributions required to explain the 
variations observed during spaceflights, and also emphasize the significance of 
close observations near the Sun, and the need for more extensive research into 
the connected solar atmosphere and its possible relationship to charged particle 
acceleration and distribution.

Due to the limited scale and linguistic homogeneity of most affective computing datasets, existing methods face challenges in generalizing emotional patterns to new languages. A proposed multi-language affective analysis framework addresses these difficulties by introducing a novel, unsupervised method for adaptating models to recognize emotions across different languages. A specific model variant was developed to tackle this problem, utilizing a contrastive learning technique that enables a single model to effectively capture universal emotional features. These features are then used in a subsequent projection layer to accommodate language-specific variations. The effectiveness of this model was demonstrated in a series of cross-lingual emotion recognition tasks, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods according to both metrics assessed: F1-score and AUC. Moreover, the proposed framework successfully applied this concept to a supervised affective analysis task within the same language, resulting in improved performance. The Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert and Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed methods are two such frameworks that provide a nuanced understanding of $k^2$-dependent decay rates in $B$ mesons. Although both approaches share a similar origin story, they have distinct differences in how they treat the $k^2$ variable and scale-breaking effects. This study compares the predictions of both frameworks within the context of $B \rightarrow D_{s} \ell \bar{\ell}$ decays, taking into account the constraints imposed by experimental data and theoretical requirements. Utilizing a likelihood ratio, the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert framework is found to be favored over the Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed model by approximately 2.5$\sigma$. The predicted differential distributions for both approaches are similarly consistent with existing measurements, yielding a slight preference for the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert framework after incorporating all available $B \rightarrow \tau \bar{\tau}$ and $B \rightarrow D_{s} \tau \bar{\tau}$ data. A novel approach is proposed to create quantum mechanical potentials that possess symmetry under the Witten anti-commutator relation, specifically one-dimensional potentials that are unobjectionable and non-singular. It is demonstrated that these potentials adhere to the polynomial Heisenberg algebra, thereby establishing a direct relationship to the harmonic oscillator. The paper investigates the complex behavior of a magnetic field line influenced by turbulent plasma through the application of Hamiltonian dynamics. In a varience of the ideal MHD model, the additional damping or driving forces are matched in strength to the plasma pressures, resulting in the calculation of over time evolving field line trajectories. This study reveals the existence of positive Lyapunov exponents in systems with marginally stable equilibrium, indicating the existence of chaotic motion and complex dynamics. Furthermore, an analysis of the energy spectrum reveals the presence of a scaling phenomenon, specifically a spectral index equal to 3, indicating a connection to the energy conservation properties and the distribution of initial conditions. Additionally, non-thermal velocity measurements follow a Lorentzian distribution, and there is evidence of periodic motion in some cases. This study demonstrates the emergence of chaotic behavior in magnetic field lines influenced by turbulent plasma, and the impact of the surrounding plasma's properties on the dynamics. It has been observed that even in situations with multiple stable equilibria, there is always at least one unstable equilibrium, and the system's dynamics are defined by only a few positive Lyapunov exponents, indicating extensive dynamic complexity on multiple time scales. This results in field line trajectories appearing statistically isotropic, with a specific scaling of isosurface volumes, and the connection to previous research on cosmic ray spectra is noted. This study suggests a model for the energy distribution of charged particles in space, which could be utilized for a more precise calculation of cosmic ray spectra. This knowledge also has the potential to be applied in a controlled magnetic field setting, which could provide insights into the dynamics necessary for strong positive Lyapunov exponents and chaos. This required setting would involve a specific configuration of coils that generates a magnetic field with non-periodic variations in time and space, resulting in multiple coexisting stable equilibria and a positive number of Lyapunov exponents. We investigate the impact of a non-abelian aether term on non-abelian plasma properties in high temperatures. Based on the gauge gravity correspondence, we examine how a non-abelian aether influences non-abelian properties of a plasma at high temperatures, specifically its near-equilibrium behavior. A non-abelian aether term leads to a deviation from the conventional Stefan-Boltzmann law, with the aether's contribution depending on the aether's self-interaction. We also study how this term affects the Casimir energy in a non-compactified AdS spacetime. Modifications to the Casimir energy result from the aether's self-interaction, with the energy being proportional to the aether's $\alpha'$-corrected free energy in the aether theory. A $\alpha'$-corrected AdS spacetime's Faddeev-Popov determinant contributes to the Casimir energy as well. If the aether's self-interaction allows for a conformally invariant energy density, the Casimir energy remains unchanged, indicating its sensitivity to the aether's specific dynamics. We also examine a $\alpha'$-corrected AdS spacetime with a non-compactified extra dimension, finding that the energy density becomes proportional to the square of the extra dimension's radius, with the pre-factor depending on the aether's free energy. A non-compactified extra dimension's impact on the Casimir energy results in a logarithmic dependence on the extra dimension's radius. We have thus demonstrated how a non-abelian aether's self-interaction influences the non-abelian plasma's behavior in high temperatures and its associated Casimir energy in various spacetime configurations. The role of a non-compactified extra dimension on the Casimir energy is also examined. The employed AdS gravity's $\alpha'$-corrections are in the context of Fierz-Pauli action. The research's results are applicable to diverse non-abelian gauge groups, with the specific case of $SU(N)$'s $\alpha'$-corrected AdS spacetime being extensively examined. The way a non-compactified extra dimension affects the Casimir energy is similarly universal and applicable to any non-compactified extra dimension. The paper's findings are relevant to diverse physical scenarios, including string theory's non-compactified extra dimensions and the AdS/CFT correspondence. The key innovation lies in a newly derived multi-asset risk-neutral stochastic integral formula, which efficiently determines the expected liquidity cost through a linear combination of asset prices at multiple horizons. This result significantly speeds up costly Monte Carlo simulations, yielding a $n$-fold increase in calculation efficiency when hedging strategies are optimized for multiple horizons. The study also establishes closed-form expressions for various market risk metrics, thereby bypassing the necessity for further Monte Carlo simulations to estimate hedging costs and corresponding risk levels. The resulting integrated framework is thereby marked by a substantial reduction in computational costs, enabling the simulation of complex hedging scenarios and subsequent calculation of corresponding risk levels with relative ease. A real-world application using high-frequency stock price data reveals an impressive 1000 times decrease in simulation efficiency when hedging strategies are optimized over multiple horizons. In this example, integrated risk and liquidity metrics accurately captured the volatility of hedging costs, thereby demonstrating the practical value of this framework in real-world hedging settings. In particular, this study finds that expected shortfall and expected liquidity cost exhibit distinct dynamics when considering multiple horizons, thereby highlighting the importance of accounting for time horizons when calculating risk levels. A generation's socioeconomic status is substantially determined by the opportunities allocated to its older members, yet allocating chances fairly across different age groups poses a significant challenge, especially when considering an infinite time frame and multiple generations. This study develops a mechanism for equitable distribution of opportunities that maintains each generation's relatively high socioeconomic status while ensuring future statuses continue to improve, even in an infinite context. This approach generates a hierarchical socioeconomic structure that mimics the pattern of overlapping generations and provides a framework for analyzing its societal implications. Furthermore, it enables an assessment of policy interventions aimed at improving chance allocation and, by extension, future socioeconomic outcomes. Numerical examples and theoretical evidence obtained through the use of advanced mathematical analysis techniques support the study's findings. These methods, which leverage acyclic graphs and the concept of recursive utility, facilitate an examination of the relationship between chance allocation and future socioeconomic statuses through the lens of generational relationships. This study's contribution is particularly relevant to fields of public economics and demography. The developed model can be viewed as a sophisticated extension of previous research on fair income distribution across different age groups. The study's results have been published in a paper that appeared in the Journal of Economic Theory, Volume 184. The related research that was published in a paper in the Journal of Economic Theory, Volume 184, explores the idea of intergenerational equity in a infinite context and presents a mechanism that prioritizes the maximization of the present value of future socioeconomic statuses while adhering to the fair allocation principles laid out by Fleurbaey and Manzanese in their 2017 paper in the Economic Letters journal. The model developed in this study can be seen as an enhancement of the static model presented by Fleurbaey and Manzanese in their 2017 paper in the Economic Letters journal and shares similarities with the dynamic model discussed by Fleurbaey, Manzanese, and Tulkens in their 2019 paper in the Journal of Economic Theory, Volume 184. The beam-beam interaction in particle accelerators creates closed orbit shifts when two opposing beams pass each other. These orbit shifts have been precisely measured in various machines and could offer a direct method of detecting subtle systematic effects. We discuss how such measurements could reveal the presence of an anomalous Lorentz transformation, which might result from a geodesic deviation induced by a massive scalar field and explore its potential for revealing its properties. We examine the potential for discovering this effect via a shift in beam position measurements at places where the two beams cross each other, and calculate the required precision needed for such a detection. For example, to identify a deviation of one part in $10^{16}$ from true time dilation, a precision of one nanometer in beam size is necessary. We also consider how current particle accelerators compare in this respect and what a future collider with a precise time measurement capability might achieve. We highlight the potential for future colliders to either discover new physics that induces a necessary small imbalance in beam energies or reveal the anomalous Lorentz transformation if no new physics is found. As an example, we calculate the energy reach of a future collider that prioritizes a precise time measurement capability over high energy reach and find it extends the reach of current limits by an order of magnitude. We examine the impact of beam properties on possible observations and emphasize the significance of accurately modeling these properties. We outline potential experimental designs for detecting a geodesic deviation through beam-beam interactions and highlight the importance of incorporating realistic beam effects into background simulations for any new physics searches relying on beam geometry. We conclude by outlining possible relationships between a future collider's design and its ability to search for a geodesic deviation induced by a massive scalar field. We also examine the constraints from existing limits on variations of the fine structure constant and the need for a new search strategy that directly targets a possible effect of a massive scalar field on beam-geometry induced closed orbits. We outline our assumptions about the type of potential that could give rise to such a effect and the consequent need for a careful distinction between spontaneous and induced effects. We examine possible sources of induced effects and closed orbits and differentiate between the geometric and mass variation components of beam lifetime. We outline possible future directions, including the potential for a suitable scalar field to also induce a non-zero anomalous magnetic moment in fundamental particles and the potential for its detection in a future collider with suitable beam materials and appropriate searches. We outline the potential for a future collider to also search for a suitable scalar field directly and examine the necessary design parameters

This paper introduces a novel algorithm that enables a group of non-collusive agents to collaborate and solve a distributed optimization problem, despite the presence of malicious agents trying to disrupt communication and manipulate the protocol. The scheme ensures that the impact of these malicious actors is minimized and does not compromise the convergence of the optimization process. Theoretical analysis has shown that the proposed method achieves a near-optimal solution and reduces the impact of the malicious agents to a level that is negligible when there are insufficient malicious actors. The effectiveness of this approach is also demonstrated through a simulation involving a complex cooperative problem with multiple agents and varying levels of malicious behavior. The results reveal that the proposed algorithm successfully resists the influence of malicious agents and yields robust and secure optimal solutions. The impact of these agents on the optimization process is compared to alternative robust distributed optimization methods, highlighting the superior performance of the new algorithm, especially when dealing with a large number of malicious agents, where it reduces the additional cost of robust optimization to a negligible amount. The complex interactions between cosmological instruments and the universe they observe pose a significant challenge for accurately determining cosmological parameters. To overcome this challenge, software instruments have been developed to simulate various instrumental effects and the surrounding environment. As future instruments become increasingly sophisticated and costly to build, simulated instruments will likely play a crucial role in their development. A proposed framework aims to leverage machine learning's ability to enhance simulations by incorporating real data, which can help distinguish between genuine and artificial data. This distinction can, in turn, reveal certain instrumental parameters and potentially even cosmological ones. A hypothetical future instrument is used as an example, with a proposed simulation being refined through the incorporation of real data from a specific source, resulting in a 10 times better distinction between genuine and artificial data and enabling the retrieval of specific instrumental and cosmological parameters. This achievement demonstrates how machine learning can enhance the simulation of an instrument complex enough to study the cosmos and how it can be used to better understand instrumental and cosmological phenomena. Futhermore, various instrumental and cosmological quantities were recovered from different types of targets and different observational conditions, which is essential for future instruments that will observe a wide variety of targets in different observational modes. This approach can be applied to the development of future cosmological instruments, allowing for a more realistic simulation of the science processes, which is vital for achieving a precise determination of the cosmos' parameters. This approach also enables the simulation of irreversible scientific processes, which is necessary for the development of future instruments that are complex and costly to build. This development is future-proof, as it allows for the easy incorporation of machine learning models into the simulation of future instruments, which will become even more crucial in the future. This approach can be viewed as an innovative application of the validated simulation-based approach, which ensures that simulations are consistent with real data and the underlying physics, and thus can be trusted to simulate the behavior of the instrument accurately. This trust is crucial for future instruments that are costly to build and will be used to determine the cosmos' parameters with a high degree of precision. This approach has been developed by integrating software instruments with machine learning models that validate the simulations against real data and the underlying physics, which guarantees the integrity of the simulations and the accuracy of the science conducted with them. We investigate how automated generation of linear order trees from sentences can be optimized for various NLP subtasks by using a supervised approach to tree structure prediction. A key aspect we examine is the word ordering subtask, a fundamental component of many NLP tasks, including semantic role labeling and dependency parsing. Building on recent advances in sequence-to-sequence models, we formulate tree structure prediction as a problem of predicting a middle layer that contains the linear order of words. Evaluating different models, we find that BART exhibits superior performance when compared to a state-of-the-art unsupervised approach called the Minimum Spanning Tree model. Furthermore, our investigation reveals that BART's performance can be improved through supervised training on the word order trees for a specific corpus, achieving an F-score of 93% on the WSJ corpus, surpassing the results obtained with the unsupervised approach and the baseline model in a related partial tree linearization task called Attachment Order Learning. Our findings also demonstrate that models pre-trained on masked text can effectively capture the linear order of words even from text without explicit ordering, and that the predicted middle layer from BART demonstrates a high degree of accuracy in the word order, yielding an F-score of 87% on the WSJ corpus. Our research shows that a supervised approach to word order tree prediction is feasible and yields a significant improvement in related tasks that depend on linear order, such as attachment order learning where the improvement is 10% F-score on the WSJ corpus. Our code and models have been made publicly available at https://github.com/ghru/learning-tree-structure. Our investigation also yields an optimized threshold for the minimum spanning tree model, resulting in an F-score of 90% on the WSJ corpus, which serves as a new baseline for the related partial tree linearization task called Attachment Order Learning. Our research provides a supervised word order tree prediction framework that facilitates further research into various NLP subtasks relying on tree structure, such as semantic role labeling, dependency parsing, and discourse parsing. Our findings related to the minimum spanning tree model and the optimized threshold for the word order prediction subtask have the potential to enhance the related partial tree linearization task called Attachment Order Learning. Our attempt to apply a supervised approach to word order tree prediction for a specific corpus shows promising results and is worthy of further exploration for other corpora, particularly those with complex word orders that are not captured effectively by models pre-trained on masked text. Deepfake detection networks initially focused on a single domain have achieved significant performance, however, these results are not directly applicable to other domains. A crucial challenge arises as we deal with new, unrelated data, leading to a substantial decline in network efficacy. A promising technique called cross-stitch connectivity has been presented in the past to enhance the performance of multi-domain networks. When applied to our deepfake detection network, using cross-stitch connectivity leads to a substantial improvement in network efficacy across different domains. Furthermore, a novel domain adaptation technique called knowledge-guided graph construction is introduced to facilitate efficient knowledge transfer between domains. This technique selects the most relevant connections between domains of different types. As a result, our proposed network achieves significant performance improvements on both known and unknown data sets in various domains. The code for our proposed network is publicly available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/ali-khoshelham/sdfacedetector. The best performance achieved by our network was a 0.88% error rate in detecting deepfakes in social media platforms. The code also includes guidelines on how to adapt the proposed network for other purposes such as deepfake removal and transfer learning. The proposed network has been tested on various datasets including the FFSD20k, DDSD, and Deepfake Detection Dataset. The results obtained are as follows: on the FFSD20k dataset with a single domain network, the error rate was 5.12%, on the DDSD dataset the error rate was 3.45%, and on the Deepfake Detection Dataset the error rate was 0.88%. The code has been designed to facilitate easy adaptation of the proposed network for other purposes such as removing deepfakes and transferring knowledge between domains of different types. The code also includes a report on the economic costs of creating and spreading deepfakes. The issue is viewed as a critical problem that affects various industries including social media, entertainment and affects their financial performance. The following financial data was gathered: the potential annual cost of deepfakes to the Hollywood film industry is estimated at $1 billion, the annual cost of deepfakes to the Chinese online gaming industry could reach 50 billion Chinese yuan, and the annual cost of deepfakes to social media platforms could range from $10 billion to $100 billion. Metric spaces with a defined angle function pose significant problems for conformal embeddability. Previous studies have made functions of positive angles accessible in certain types of spaces, specifically those with a feature of being locally path-connected and having a compact metric compactification as its boundary. The aim of this research was to relax the boundary condition by focusing on metric spaces with a function of positive angles and addressing the issue of conformal embeddability. The study demonstrated that a space with a function of positive angles can be transformed into a stronger analytic structure, specifically a conformal metric structure, provided it satisfies a specific topological requirement, is locally compact, and has a specific property called the chain property. The development of a conformal metric structure enables the resolution of the problem of conformal embeddability. The research also introduces the concept of a angle-modified inner metric, a useful tool for achieving the defined conformal metric structure. The relationship between this new metric and the original one is explored, along with an examination of its properties. The study on a function of positive angles also includes an examination of its relationship with a different type of function, known as the inner function of positive angles. The interaction between these two functions is explored, along with an examination of the spaces defined by them and the connection between them. The final part of the study delves into the assignment of a value to the angle function at the boundary of a specific type of space, enabling the extension of its defined domain to its entire metric compactification as a boundary. The study concludes by examining the connection between this assigned value and the concept of a delta-angle, also exploring its relationship with the inner function of positive angles. The connection between a function of positive angles and the concept of a delta-angle serves as the foundation for deriving important topological information about its defined domain. The research demonstrated that a space with a function of positive angles and specific topological characteristics can be divided into distinct parts, each containing a specific type of point, including those whose surrounding environment resembles a line, those whose surrounding environment is similar to a circle with a small gap, and those whose surrounding environment is similar to an n-sided polygon. The relationship between a function of positive angles and the concept of a delta-angle also enables the derivation of important boundary information for a specific type of space. A new type of pyramid scheme, incorporating financial transactions has been discovered, utilizing a decentralized system. This study examines user behavior on a large-scale pyramid scheme known as Forsage, analyzing its internal workings and the financial consequences for its participants. Utilizing transaction data from Ethereum, Forsage's transactions were identified and its scheme structure reconstructed. A wallet's position within the scheme was determined by tracking referral relationships and calculating return on investment. A total of 87,247 Ethereum wallets participated in Forsage, with 13,804 receiving investments and 74,443 investing in the scheme. A statistical analysis of user losses revealed that 85% of participants experienced financial losses, with the median loss equivalent to the ether value of 4.6 non-methuselah transactions. A comparison of Forsage transactions to those of Ethereum as a whole showed they followed a similar distribution pattern, except for a significant peak at zero loss. This implies that the majority of users who experience losses do not invest again, contributing to the scheme's limited growth. A examination of transaction timing revealed that Forsage transactions are clustered into short periods of intense activity, suggesting users time their investments carefully to maximize returns. A simulation of a user who invests immediately after account creation showed a significant increase in chances of experiencing minimal losses, whereas a user who waits until completing ten transactions has an 80% chance of experiencing minimal losses. A further analysis of user behavior found that 5.3% of participants re-invest their gains, with a majority of these gaining minimal losses, and 1.3% gaining significant losses. A comparison of user demographics to those of the overall Ethereum user base showed that Forsage participants have similar address ages but a higher percentage of non-methuselah addresses, suggesting an experienced user base. A comparison of transaction amounts revealed that Forsage participants spend a similar total amount of ether but distribute it more unequally, with a larger portion going to a smaller group of users. A final analysis estimated the total ether circulating within the Forsage scheme as 2,536,577, with a median user investment of 0.45 ether. Based on this data, it is estimated that the Forsage scheme has the potential to incur significant financial losses for the majority of its participants, with the potential to attract more users and increase losses before it ultimately collapses. A comparison to other pyramid schemes shows that Forsage has a higher chance of experiencing minimal losses and a lower chance of experiencing significant losses, contributing to its limited growth. The Milky Way's globular cluster population remains inadequately mapped, particularly in the first galactic quadrant. The VVV survey has filled this gap in infrared imagery, allowing the discovery of 11 new potential globular clusters. The study presents a re-examination of ten previously suspected globular clusters in the VVV survey database and VLT/MUSE spectroscopy. By analyzing their structural and chemical characteristics, the study limits were narrowed to three objects that exhibit globular cluster properties: VVV CL1, VVV CL3, and VVV CL4. A comprehensive study of these clusters reveals a broad age range, with VVV CL1 and VVV CL4 both appearing young, at 7-10% of the Milky Way's age, while VVV CL3 is older, at 60-80% of the Milky Way's age. The study notes that both VVV CL1 and VVV CL4 exhibit double main sequence patterns, indicating they could be young massive clusters similar to NGC 2173 and NGC 6457. If confirmed, VVV CL1 and VVV CL4 would join the small group of young massive clusters within the Milky Way. The study suggests their small size might have escaped detection until recently, thanks to the high sensitivity of the VVV survey in the infrared band. The study further notes that both VVV CL1 and VVV CL4 reside in molecular clouds, which could have influenced their development. The research implies that young massive clusters, particularly those situated in the Milky Way's bulge, may have distinct populations with distinct lifetimes. While both VVV CL1 and VVV CL4 probably won't survive another billion years, they hold significant value in understanding the formation and evolution of the Milky Way's bulge. The study estimates that both clusters have a total mass of a few thousand solar masses and model projections suggest they could shed some light on the Milky Way's early history if studied further. The study closes by highlighting the need to continue observing these clusters with high spatial and spectral resolution, either through the use of improved infrared surveys or dedicated spectroscopic studies, which could provide a deeper understanding of the Milky Way's evolution, particularly its bulge region. The research identifies VVV CL3 as the oldest cluster in the sample, with a distance of 6.5 kiloparsecs from the Sun and an absolute magnitude of -3.5. To gain insights that can drive improvement in complex business processes, it is essential to analyze past data, especially data containing errors or inconsistencies. This research focuses on using historical information to estimate the overall performance and accuracy of a business process's stages, even when some stages' predictions are incorrect. A key finding shows that the average model performance can be calculated as 1 times the overall accuracy plus the number of stages times the difference between the overall accuracy and the accuracy of a single stage. A similar result applies to the average of a stage's precision, which can be calculated as the overall precision plus the number of stages times the difference between the overall precision and a single stage's precision. A numerical example demonstrates how these formulas work in practice. To validate these findings, experiments were conducted using multiple machine learning models and datasets. The results provided in the research can be useful for process analysts and supervisors seeking to assess model performance in complex processes with multiple stages. We provide detailed analysis on functions belonging to Gelfand-Shilov spaces $S^m \cap P_\sigma$, examining how their growth is related to the growth of their Fourier transforms. By applying the method of stationary phase, we derive fundamental estimates on asymptotic expansions of integrals with oscillatory factors. These estimates are linked to the characteristics of functions within $S^m \cap P_\sigma$, specifically their smoothness and growth properties. As a broader contribution, we establish the relationship between the smoothness of functions in Gelfand-Shilov spaces and the order of the resulting integrals following the application of the stationary phase method. Moreover, we demonstrate the convergence of a specific series of functions, which has ramifications for the analysis of pseudodifferential operators within these spaces of analysis. Furthermore, we investigate the connection between the order of these spaces and the characteristics of pseudodifferential operators, ultimately establishing their connection to the order of the derivatives involved. This investigation provides a necessary foundation for the study of microlocal analysis within the context of Gelfand-Shilov spaces. As an example of the benefits of this analysis, we consider the example of recovering a function from its moments, examining how the recovery process relates to the characteristics of the spaces in question and how this is linked to the order of polynomial growth that characterizes these spaces. This investigation offers a stepping stone for the examination of fundamental issues in the recovery of functions and the moments that result from the application of pseudodifferential operators within these spaces of analysis. This research also offers a necessary foundation for the investigation of the extension of results related to the Paley-Wiener theorem and the properties of the Fourier transform within these spaces of analysis. This knowledge can be applied to the analysis of the properties of the Fourier transform of functions belonging to the Gelfand-Shilov spaces $S^m \cap P_\sigma$ and the associated spaces of analysis $H^m \cap G_\sigma$, which have a direct connection to the characteristics of the regions $\Omega$ on which these transforms are defined. This knowledge is a necessary prerequisite for the examination of fundamental issues related to the moment problem and the properties of the Fourier transform within these spaces of analysis. This research has a broader application in the analysis of fundamental issues related to the moment problem and the properties of the Fourier transform of functions belonging to the Gelfand-Shilov spaces $S^m \cap P_\sigma$ and the associated spaces of analysis $H^m \cap G_\sigma$. Researchers observed multiple lines of hydrogen emanating from the surface of a variable star called Proxima Centauri during a significant flare. Based on historical data, it's evident that hydrogen emission varies significantly in response to different flare intensities. Typically, a broadening of the spectral lines is observed in the optical and ultraviolet spectra during flares. In the case of Proxima Centauri, however, the 1215.673 Angstrom line of hydrogen showed an unusually small shift in spectrum, which cannot be explained by the high energy emitted in the flare. A model suggesting that hydrogen is emitted from a deeper, cooler layer of the star during strong flares could account for the observed line broadening and shift in the ultraviolet spectrum. This interpretation is supported by the decreased emission in the ultraviolet spectrum after the flare and the corresponding decrease in energy emitted in the surface layers. If confirmed, this finding could provide a better understanding of how hydrogen behaves in the atmospheres of low-mass stars even in the absence of a flare. Additionally, the analysis of continuum spectrum during the flare revealed that the increased brightness in the ultraviolet spectrum is limited to a specific range and does not extend to higher frequencies, which may indicate that the flare is confined to a specific height in the photosphere. The study of hydrogen line broadening during the flare also challenges existing radiation models and could potentially influence the estimation of stellar energy balances, particularly those of the coolest M-dwarf stars. If the unusual behavior of hydrogen line broadening is verified through further observation, it could offer valuable insights into the radiative transfer processes in the atmospheres of low-mass stars and possibly vary with different levels of magnetic activity. The current evidence suggests that large flares can create conditions where the outer layers of the star are largely neutral, resulting in a permanent hydrogen emission in the ultraviolet spectrum. The duration and intensity of this emission depend on the mass and level of magnetic activity of the star. The study of Proxima Centauri during multiple flares has demonstrated that even the smallest and coolest fully convective star can exhibit behavior similar to more massive low-luminosity stars like AD Leo and YZ Ceti, which was initially thought to be driven by different physical processes. The findings encourage further observation of hydrogen emission in the ultraviolet spectrum during flares on similar low-mass stars to determine the frequency of neutral hydrogen emission in the upper atmospheres of these stars and the factors that influence its occurrence. Compared to geometric models, point cloud models are more resilient to certain image transformations, yet they also suffer from a vulnerability to scale-invariant shifts, which can significantly impact their accuracy when deployed in safety-critical applications. To address this limitation, we introduce a new framework called Twisted PC (TPC) that incorporates information about scale-invariant shifts into the model's predictions. Specifically, TPC predicts both the geometric features and the underlying shifting factor, which represents the distance from a point to the shifting surface. When combined with standard PC models, this additional prediction proves beneficial, and when applied to scale-aware predictions, it yields an improvement of up to $13.1\%$ in accuracy. Moreover, our proposed method significantly simplifies the sampling process for surface representation, reducing the number of point cloud samples by a factor of ten. The code and results for our Twisted PC framework are available at: \url{https://github.com/autointel/TPC}. When applied to various 3D computer vision tasks, TPC achieves superior performance on datasets, with an increase in accuracy of up to $18.1\%$ for SGS and $13.1\%$ for PlaneSeg. When applied to self-supervised learning, TPC leads to a $26.8\%$ gain in certified accuracy against scale-invariant shifts for PointCloudPCN. The development of the TPC framework also enables the creation of a new dataset with artificially added scale-invariant shifts, which can be utilized by the community for the fair comparison of future safe PC models. When used on this new dataset, PointCloudPCN yields an improvement of up to $18.1\%$ in accuracy. The code for the Twisted PC dataset, which was generated using the DD3D simulator, is available at: \url{https://github.com/autointel/TPC-Dataset}. The design and simulation of sensors without safe PC models as reference are also possible using the TPC framework, which is now part of the Open 3D Simulator Framework (O3DSF). The RPA method has been successfully applied to investigate the quantum states derived from the collective model, particularly the pole corresponding to the electric dipole giant resonance in $^{16}$O. However, the RPA formalism is prone to instability issues due to the non-hermitian nature of the Hamiltonian, compounded by the approximation used to obtain the discrete spectrum. A new approach has been developed to address these challenges, involving a hermitian Hamiltonian obtained through a unitary transformation of the original RPA Hamiltonian. This hermitian Hamiltonian is then used to determine the RPA poles, and the resulting spectrum is free from the artificial splitting of complex poles. The proposed method also enables the calculation of transition strengths accurately, and it has been demonstrated that the hermitian RPA spectrum is equivalent to the original non-hermitian spectrum. The application of this method to the $^{16}$O RPA states reveals that the hermitian Hamiltonian yields a clearer picture of the collective states associated with the giant resonances, and it facilitates the distinction between the $1^{-}$ and $2^{+}$ states that otherwise appear as a complex conjugate pair of poles. The proposed hermitian RPA formalism provides a meaningful interpretation of the Schrödinger picture RPA results and offers valuable insights into the nature of the poles arising from the RPA Hamiltonian. The hermitian RPA approach has been compared with alternative methods intended to alleviate the non-hermitian RPA challenges, and it has been found that these methods essentially replicate the hermitian transformation. The proposed approach has been tested using both realistic interactions and the Wood-Saxon potential, and it has been demonstrated to yield unbiased results. The hermitian RPA method has been further utilized to investigate the oscillation modes in $^{16}$O and $^{24}$Mg, and it has been found to be particularly effective in differentiating between the complex conjugate pairs of poles arising from the RPA Hamiltonian. Nonlinear dynamical systems often exhibit complex behaviors that linearized models can't capture fully, making it difficult to analyze their stability and patterns. Recently, the Koopman operator framework has gained popularity for analyzing nonlinear systems using their invariant manifolds, and has been linked to the use of spectral methods for studying their stability. Utilizing this relationship, we have developed a method of investigating the stability of nonlinear systems using their Koopman operators and mode metric computations. This approach enables us to study both the short-term and long-term behaviors of these systems and have applied it to several examples. Furthermore, we have observed that this method is particularly effective in examining the stability of systems with invariant manifolds maintained by nonlinear damping mechanisms, such as those found in globally coupled oscillators and a laser system, when traditional spectral methods fail. This research demonstrates how the Koopman operator framework and mode metric computations can be used to analyze nonlinear systems that have nonlinear damping processes maintaining their invariant manifolds, and paves the way for further exploration of these systems on both the theoretical and experimental fronts. This study highlights how the mode imperfection ratio can be used to assess the effects of nonlinear damping processes on these systems, either systems with a limited number of degrees of freedom or those described by partial differential equations, when the nonlinear interactions are weak. This research also introduces a new method of computing mode metric computations for a wide class of nonlinear systems, particularly those with invariant manifolds maintained by nonlinear damping processes, for which traditional mode metric computations fail, by analyzing the evolution of the mode imperfection ratio over time rather than system dynamics directly. This approach has been successfully applied to several nonlinear systems with various types of nonlinear damping processes maintaining their invariant manifolds, including a laser system, a system of globally coupled oscillators, and a system with a nonlinear boundary condition, when traditional spectral methods fail. This research demonstrates how the mode imperfection ratio can be used to assess the effects of nonlinear damping processes on these systems when traditional spectral methods fail, either because the Koopman operator has a non-simple spectrum or because the mode metric computations fail. This study paves the way for further exploration of these systems on both the theoretical and experimental fronts, and highlights how the mode imperfection ratio can be used as a control target to achieve stability in nonlinear systems with nonlinear damping processes maintaining their invariant manifolds. When integrated into the attention mechanism of a sequence generator, this approach yields a sentence selection pattern that correlates with the semantic meaning of input sentences. Experimental evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate substantial gains in performance, with improvements of up to 13% in certain cases. Our findings also highlight the diversity of sentence selection patterns that are both highly structured and dependent on modeling conditions, thereby providing valuable operational and theoretical insights into sentence selection itself. Our SparseGAN framework serves as a general-purpose solver that can be used to demonstrate both the necessity of sentence selection and the importance of modeling conditions in neural text generation. The concept of interstellar panspermia is highly plausible, suggesting that life could be extending beyond Earth by enabling microbial life to thrive in the vast space and allowing it to adapt to various environments. Assessing this hypothesis requires examining how stellar phenomena affect the viability of microbial life in planetary systems' outer reaches. A comprehensive analysis of UV, X-ray, and high-energy radiation from nearby stars reveals that specific environments are more likely to facilitate the spread of life through panspermia, specifically being supported by findings from the $Chandra$ X-ray Observatory, showcasing the diverse effects different stars have on the interstellar medium through mass loss caused by solar winds, wind interactions, and supernovae explosions. A better understanding of how radiation affects microbial life and the development of a viability index can both help evaluate the potential for life to survive the journey as panspermia. This study paves the way for a comprehensive assessment of Earth's biocentric environment and others similar to it, offering a foundation for exploring the possibility of life spreading through panspermia in our cosmos. Finally, considering the variety of solar systems supported by such stars, this study also examines the possibility of finding life elsewhere in the cosmos through panspermia, extending the scope to searching for life on planets and on interstellar comets. A comprehensive examination of these targets is presented in the companion paper by Huggins et al. (2023). This study focuses on searching for biosignatures on planets and on interstellar combs, while the search for life on exoplanets is more extensively covered in other works, such as those listed in the extragalactic astronomy Preston et al. (2020) and astrophysical panspermia references in Huggins et al. (2023). This study reveals the most promising solar systems for searching for life on planets and on interstellar comets, recommending targeted observations with upcoming missions such as the James Webb Space Telescope and the Terrestrial Planet Finder. A necessary step for finding life elsewhere in the cosmos is understanding how life can spread through panspermia, which involves examining the interplay between solar radiation, the viability of microbial life, and the movement of comets and planets. A key finding presented in the paper shows that specific types of nearby stars support the spread of life through panspermia, which is further explored in the companion paper by examining the variety of solar systems supported by these stars and searching for life on the planets and comets within them. Accurate population density measurements are crucial for understanding various animal populations and their habits. Traditionally, animal populations have been studied using traditional capture-recapture methods, although these methods have limitations when it comes to accounting for movement and localized studies of a specific area. The emergence of capture-recapture methods based on spatial information has addressed these limitations, enabling researchers to estimate population densities within specific areas, while also taking into consideration movement patterns among those populations. These advances in methods have created opportunities to study various complex behaviors among animals, including those related to food sources and community dynamics. A simulation-based evaluation of the SCR method's accuracy has shown that it performs well even under challenging conditions of low population densities and low success rates in capturing animals. Furthermore, model robustness has been validated through a lack of significant differences in estimated population densities obtained using various model assumptions, in comparison to actual known densities. The proposed SCR method has been successfully applied to a real-life study of a mountain goat population in North America, yielding a population density estimate of 9 animals per square kilometer within a specific area of study, while also providing useful insights into movement patterns among those goats. Overall, the proposed SCR method provides a useful tool for conducting animal studies at a localized scale, while accurately estimating population densities and shedding light on movement patterns among those populations.
